Uv DZAII NELLIE, There has been little to mark the difference between the winter and summet chapeaux this season, both colours and mate/lab. being of the lightest and most airy nature pes• sible ; but though tulle, chiffon, and lace have been pre-eminent on our hats of late, the straw toque or hat has been reserved till its proper season. Straws, wide and spreading at the sides and in the front, are to be turned up sharply at the back instead of being pressed down on the hair behind in the exaggerated and universal manner which became so common last year, and trimmed with large, wide bows, clusters of flowers, or a cachepeigne of lace, falling in fluted ends gracefully behind. Plain round shapes in straw, with the brim rolled up and the straw crown gathered into folds, held down in front will, gold or cameo clasps, are somewhat novel for morning wear, worn tipped well forward in front, higher behind than before.

There is no doubt that black di whether in cloth, crêpe-tie-chine, voile, or canvas, will be very much worn. The expectation that very bright oclours are to be worn does not seem to be authorised. On the contrary, the tendency of the hOur is for white, cream, ivory, and the palest and softest in pastel tints of colour. Yellow seems to be coming in again for dress purposes. Grey is in high favour for both day and evening wear, but white is almost absolutely certain to be the principal wear durina this season, and black will run it pretty close. With a black gown any colour can be worn in trimmings and, what is more to the purpose, any hat can be donned, regardless of what its colours may be. Black cloth is always smart, and it does not data' like coloured gowns. The texture of summer cloth is now as supple and as light as cashmere and it drapes as easily, a very great advantage w4ll the clinging kind of dress now Prollli
tresses,

A charming pale blue cloth dress is trimmed with guipure in cream colour, and finished with a sigh guipure collar. The fold down the back of the bodice is a new feature, and a graceful addi- tion. It is carried down to the waist over the high slack satin shaped belt, and the bodice is finished 'hove it with guipure in bolero fashion. The hnnts are outlined with guipure, widening as it rises, and almost covering the shoulders. The sleeves are finished with guipure, and on the skirt t complete tablier is outlined with the lace. This lesign, too, is admirably suited to summer tex- tures and such filmy materials as soft satin, silk aruslin, chiffon, striped gauzes, and English crapes, ttc. The lace may be light or heavy in character, to suit the class of fabric.

Some --pie keep gowns a long time, and therefore require them to be in the latest mode to start with. A short dress in grey cloth or zibeline has a pleated skirt and pleated bolero. At the top these latter pleats are held down by velvet tabs, outlined with black and gold, and finished with tassels to match. The diagonally-striped waistcoat is cut low to show a stitched chemisotte of white silk, the collar matching it. Bands of black velvet, bordered with gold cord, finish the sleeves; and the shaped belt is black velvet. The pleats on the skirt flow out a little below the knee-line, and aro edged with stitching or rows of braid. This dress, if made in voile or homespun, for summer wear, could have black satin substi- tuted for the heavier black velvet for both belt and trimmings, and narrow ribbon for trimming the edge of the pleats. The form of both skirt and bodice is applicable to almost any material, such as alpaca, canvas, drill, or zephyr, but in the case of saeh light summer materials as these the heavy cuffs and the brace-like trimmings on the shoulders would be out of character, and could be replaced by lace or ribbons. It seems as though the full, pleated bolero were going to have a great success this year. It is seen on afternoon and evening gowns, and has always a most graceful street.
Your loving, JENNIR.

Multitudes of seagulls visit the London Thames every winter, and the announcement that a millinery house bad given an order for ten thousand seagull's wings, for the trimming of hats recently elicited an intimation from the Bing and Queen, that their Majesties would do I all in their power to put down the practice of slaughter- ing birds for the sake of their plumage. It is perhaps no more cruel to kill birds for their feathers, than to kill them for food, but the feathers and wings of many kites killed for the latter purpose, might well satisfy all the demands of fashion. At any rate it seems a pity to lacrifice the seagulls, as the birds are not only a popular feature of the riverside, bet also round our coasts where they aid the fishermen by indicating the presence of the shoals of fish. The King. whilst paying a week-end visit to Lord and Lady Burton, at Rangernore Hall, went over the famous Bass Brewery at Burton-or-Trent, and the occa- sion recalls the story that is told about his Majesty owir g his life to a glass of beer. At the turning-poiot in his all but fatal attack of fever, his Majesty, then Prince of Wales, fancied a glass of beer, and though it was not without risk, this was given hien. Happily it turned out well, and his Majesty is popularly suppesed to owe his recovery in no small degree to his own sug- gestion. The King has therefore a great appreciation of what Is sometimes called the national beverage, and once before in 1888 be visited the Allsopp Brewery at Burton-on-Trent; Except aroonoct High Church felk, there is a dispos'- tion in society circles to disregard the restrictions of Lent. Many eelf-denyiog people not only foreswear meat and delicacies, but amusements of all kinds during this season, and even amongst the worldlings belle used to be tabooed. This year, however, many dances are being given, and other social arrangements, such ao dinners, plays, and political parties, are going on as usual. Easter falls early, and when April comes society will make one mad rush to crowe as much as possible into the three months that will remain before the Coronation heralds the wanton of the London season. The woman who dresses well never wears felt head- gear, after the beginning of March, straws come in theta and leading milliners are showing their new models. These turn up sharply at the back, instead of down,and are wide and spreading at the sides and in front. Lace is freely employed to trim them, an effective vsil-like drapery sometimes surrounding tbe brims, at others falling in fluted ends gracefully behind. Generally speaking, the lace is coarse, delicate cobweb, however costly, heing by no meaty; so successful as the variety which is bold of outline, and coarse of thread. Regard- ing flowers, cowslips and primulas are tbe favourite+ blooms of the momont,but alas, the colours are distract- ing:and when mauve,purple, and magenta, for example meet in one room, one longs for the days when tee crude suggestions that herald the after Easter fashions, will have yielded to wiser second thoughts. There are few more handsome combinations than black ard gold when wiaely blended. Some of the newest " round" sailor cellars are of gold tissue with block passornenterie laid on them. The rich =eerie] shines tbrouoh the meahes, and in and out the scrolls with excellent effect. The passementerie is somewhat large in design, and the collar is either left with the natural outlines of the pattern, or is edged with lace or kilted chiffon. Similar trimming over silver tissue is net so much appreciated, nor is cream paasementerie so effective as the black. Industrious workers might well contrive eollare and revers from stars and wheels worked with black silk twist in crochet; they could have as bold a pattern as they liked at comparatively little exertion, and the expense would be nothing like that of the manu- factured article. The basque has been slowly creeping into favour for POMO time past, to the horror of all hut the quite slim It is however, amenable to so many modifications that no anxiety need really he felt, even by the mast " abundant" among us. For these " unfortunates," it should take upon itself the semblance of coat tails, cut square, or rounded off like a man's morning coat. To the slim, the most becoming baeque is that which reaches to only a few inches below the waist, rounded and fluted, when it is jaunty and trim. There is again some talk of hip paniers,but up to the present few lead- ing Society women have patronised them. ' Viyella cloth is in greater favor than ever for mornirg and smart afternoon blouses, but it is to be feared that net infrequently the uninitiated fail to get what they pay for. Not long since the Manufacturers of this beautiful cloth were forced to bring an action againat a firm of drapers, who were found to be passing off fabric under the name of Viyella, it being nothing of the kind. By turning to the aelvedga however, one can quickie tell if the cloth be genuine or not, for if the former it bears the " " label with which the majority of us are thoroughly familiar. Net evening blouses may be wonderfolly smartened by those wbo can crochet. The newest idea is not to make boleros, and heavy trimmings, but dainty little flowers and stars in coloured silks, which are sewn down at intervals as a powdering. Only the middle of each blossom is secured, the petals beino left free to curl a little and make natural shadows. Pink Tudor roses on white net, gold and green, or pink and blue stars, on a black net ground,are to be recommended. Each applique must be no larger than a shilling, and if it smaller so much the better, and the colours must be ruled by moderation and by the hue of the silk slip. So many women ruin their mental and physical health by taking drugs that restrictions cannot be made too severe with regard to the sale of morphine and all such deleterious preparations, In Paris an action for darn- I ages has been taken against a cilemist who supplied morphine to a lady without a medical prescription. A I similar warning is needed over here, and increased diffi- culties might well be placed in the way of obtaining these soul-destroying drugs. They should only be sup- plied on a medical prescription, and this should be stamped by the chemist each time, so that it could only be made up at the prcper intervals. The latest afternoon frivolity is a competition to see NO' o can purchase the most for a penny. Any article Or articles will serve, so long as not more than a penny has been expended ; sucn as, say, a farthing worth each of soap, candles, matches and washir g soda. As each guest arrives, the purchases are exhibited and the prize awarded to the visitor who has produced the most good for the fixed capital outlay. The amusement depends upon the variety of articles diplayed, but it can scarcely be called an intellectual diversion, thought it migl t, perhapa,lsometimee afford a useful lessen in practical economy. MADGE.

MISS FOSBROOKE'S PORTRAIT,
J. MACLAREN COBBAN (Author of " The King of Andaman," 0..)
CHAPTER I.

On the first floor of number thirteen of one of those fine squares of central London which fashion long ago affected there lived Claude Cunningham and his wife. The number was the most lall• lucky of numbers, and the square was said to be the most unfortunate of squares (at least to persons of Claude's pursuit), but the young couple were so happy and BO hopeful that they thought they could afford to laugh at superstitions which cast a deeper gloom on the disappointed and despondent. Claude was a painter gaily resolved to distinguish himself, and Claude's wife as also resolved, though With a more equable eheerfuhiess, that no effort should be wanting on her part to make that day soon dawn when her hush:l7nd should awake to find himsalt famous. _ _ _

The large front room with a north light was studio, drawing-room and dining-room all in one, and about seven o'clock on a certain day towards the end of the year Claude stood before the tel mantel-mirror in evening dress. Two candles burned in a branched candle-Stick of wrought iros on either side of the glass, and by their light his seriously considered the set .of his neck-tie and at- the same time noted the poise of his fine head and shoulders: he had an abundance of curly, reddish- golden hair, and a flowing moustache of the same colour.
"No, that won't do," he said, and straightway undid the bow.

7'7l:et-me, try it," said his wife ; and he turned at once and stooped a little towards her (for he was considerably taller than she), and let her nar.nipulaisi the neck-tie. " There " said she, "that's lovely: aeither too tight' nor too flat, butjust soft and easy." . ..
. . . "But are_ you sure," said he, turning agaia to the glass, "that it won't come undone ?" "Did you ever P" she asked in a mock-tragia tone, "know anything of mine to turn out a failure ?"
He looked at her with a loving, indulgent smile. "Well, no; I'm not a failure yet, am I ?" " Don't talk nonsense, Claude," said she, more seriously. "And be quick or - you'll be late for dinner.' _
" I don't half like going without you, Dolly," said he. "I wish you had been asked." "Don't be absurd, Claude, dear. How. could I have been asked when your friend doesn't blow my existence ?"

"No," said he, and he looked at her Somewhat wistfully, as if he wondered whetyr there was any soreness in her heart. " Come, Claude," said she ; " be late." go he finished arraying himself, and went. And when he was gone his wife sat down by the Are in a brown study. What was to come of tha* night's adventure ? Great things, they both hoped. It was for them a notable occasion—a point of depart- ure. .Claude had been casually introduced soma little while before in the studio of a far more fam- ous artist than himself to Lady Fosbrooke, who was known to be very wealthy and to be a liberal patron of Art, and, close upon the introduction, he. had received an invitation to dinner,—an invitation which he had that night gone to 'fulfil, and from which he hoped that ultimately a commission might come. A well-paid commission was his constant dream; for, though he and his wife were cheerful and content with each other, they were poor. They had hastily married for love about a year ago, after an acquaintance of two or three months. They had first met in the National Gal- lery, where Dolly had been in the habit of going on "Students' days" to copy pictures, and whither Claude had chanced to go to study a certain mas- terpiece of portraiture on his return from a course of the Art 'Schools of Paris. They married, though they had little but their hopes to live upon; but, as Claude truly enough said, that was a more sustain- ing diet eaten together than devoured apart. They lid not blazon abroad their marriage to all the world, because they had to arrange it with great ec- anomy and, second, because they could not afford to, receive and entertain people. Therefore they rented the first-floor of number thirteen—(although it cost more than they could well pay ; but Claude declared he must have for studio a room that was large and lofty)—and they lived there and worked' titer* together in the supreme satisfaction of love. Claude painted pictures for posterity, and Dolly drew things in black-and-white for the actual needs of mag- azines and hooks. 4611 y adored her husband, and admired his work, but with the keen„ practical sense of a loving woman she had soon perceived that he knew neither how best-to apply his talent nor hovr to push 'himself in the market " You are just a big, beautiful steam-engine, Claude, my dear," she had said to him once. And he had had the wit to reply. "Well, Dolly, I don't object to let you drive me," Thus Dolly now sat, with the toe of her little slipper pointed at the fire, and thought over all these goings and smiled at some of them. "Ile is a dear, big, good natured boy," she said to herself, " and I love him! I love him !" She was a little sad that she sat alone now as on former occasions, but shs told herself not to be " silly," for had shenot urged him to go here' and go there, fo accept invitations, and to become known', without insisting that she should become known too, shim they could not at present entsrtain in return ? She had made up her mind to make her husband recognised as a great artist—to drive her " engine " well—and to that end she had per- suaded him that his forte was portrait -painting, and that therefore he must make acquaintances in society. "'Don't be a fool," she said to herself, rising and sitting down at the table to iinialt a drawing. "Don't grumble because • things are going just as you wanted them to go." She worked on at herdiawing. By and bye she rose, went to the side-board and took from it some sold viands, and with them and, a glass of water she sat down again at her work. And so she ate and drew. Her simple supper finished, she still went on with her drawing till distant clocks hung high in the air boomed out eleven—(she paused to count the strokes)—and the swfft night cabs began to, roll through the ,iquare carrying theatre-goers home. Still she worked on, till the pencil was ready to drop from her numbed fingers, and her eyes Relied with the desire for sleep. Then she straightened her weary bacjt, 'rose and put her work away, and after having golte into the bedroom which opened off the studio to don a warm dressing-gown she sat clown by the dying fire to await her husband's return. Twelve , o'clock was sleepily and sonorously booming from Big Ben of Westminster when she heard his step on the pavement, and his hand on the street dour. Then she jumped up to meet him. He had sprung up the stairs so quickly and 80 many steps at a time that she was in his arms before he bad well opened the door. "How late you are,' she said when, they, were in and the door was shut.
-7; f-cWidn;tilelTit, Dolly," said he ; "but I wish you had been there." s "Never- mind that, Clande. Whom di/ you meet"

"Oh, of course, there was first of all Lady ros- brooke, and then there was her daughter, a most re- markable woman." He Pau" and run his hand / through his hair. "And who besides ?" she asked. " Oh, several ; but I didn't have much to say to any of them but Miss Foshrooke ; I took her into dinner, and talked with her Most of the evening—a- alarming woman." " Thts seems serious, Claude," said his wife wfilh laugh. " Tell me about her. Is she handsome ' "Yes, rather," answered Claude. " Only rather. How, then, was she remarkable and charming ?" "She talked well, and she listened well; listen- ing well isa great gift; and she really seemed to blow more about Art than I do." "I might say, Claude, that a person might do *hat without being rplarkable." "Oh, come; that's unkind, Dolly." "Yes, it is, Claude," said she. "I confesp. But tell me how she charmed you, because I should like to charm you too." "You do, my dear," said he, "not now and then, but .always." " It's very nice of you to say that, Claude. But tell me—do you think you may get a commission ?" " That's just it. She was very much interested my work, and in my plans—" "Our plans, Claude." " Yes, of course, our plans, my dear. She wants me to paint, her portrait—and she's a capital sub- ject: fine soft modelling about her face and neck —" and he played with his thumb in the air as if ha were outlining something—" almost as sat as yours, Dolly. And what do you think .1 --she said she would like to see my works !" "And what did you say ?" "What could I say but that I would Yee pleased MP show her them ij" "That may be all very charming, ']*hi; bat I don't see how it helps you towards a 6,oazinissioss,„ tear ;that mutt come from Lady Fasbrooke, maatiw't it r

"No, there's the curious thing. It is Miss Yea- lsrooke that is evidently the chief person in the house, and a man told me that it is really she that has Qui money." " Oh, then, my dear," said his wife, " that makes it a different affair."

They talked some little while longer about Miss .Fosbrooke and the painting of her portrait, and what sum. Claude might reasonably expect for his work, and then they withdrew to bed. Next meriting they again discussed the prospect of it genuine commission to paint Miss Fosorooke's portrait. • "I think it would be the making of me," said Claude. " She's a splendid subject, mid I believe I could do it justice." And he began with his thumb to indicate certain bold outlines on the table-cloth. " But" said he, "she has no hard lines: nothing but the brush could touch off her soft modelling." " Suppose, Claude," said his wife, " that you run out for a sheet of rough canvas, and get your hand in. You tell me I have softmodelling, too—" " You have," said. Claude. " Well," said his wife, " you can try this morn- ing a rough portrait of Inc.'' Claude jumped at her suggestion, and went out tstraightw ay to buy a sheet oi rough canvas. When he was gone, Dolly, in her usual morning array (in which she looked very charming) of print dress and, a large white apron, went round the roma dusting and. setting things in order. She subdued its sitting-room and dining-room aspect, and brought into relief its studio features. She set Claude's easel in its proper place for the northern light and placed near it a tittle table with his open paint- box and his brushes. She was engaged in clean sing Isis palette when a knock came to the door. Half absently, and wittLoat at all thinking who might be seeking admission, she said, " Come in." And in did Come two tail, ihsidonabiy-dressed ladies, the ono rather more thm nnddie-aged and the ,other some five ur six mid t weuty.

" is not Ale. Cunningham in ?" asked the elder, first glancing- round the room and then looking ait " .No," answered Dolly, "he is not." She was flushed by the sudden incursion ; and the style of the visitors and the suspicion that they were Lady Fosbrooke and her dathrider flushed her still more. She wondered on the instant if she should suggest that they should await Claude's return—(if they- went they nnglit not come back, and. Claude might lose a chauce)—but the ladies anticipated the sug- gestion. " We will wait for a little," said. the elder, " yen think lie will not be long." " He will be in almost at once," said Dolly. "Thank you," said they, while the elder lady sat down on a chair at band, and the younger began an interested ins:,ection of the pictures about the room. They showed no curiosity about Dolly, and. it be- gan to dawn on her that they probably took her for sonic person of the house. They could not know that he was Claude's wife ; indeed, in all likeli- hood, they did not suppose that Claude—a voung, strugeing painter, living in lodgings—could be 80 fooiis as to have a wife. With this view of herself time suddenly presented—that to these ladies she was nobody, and if anybody an encumbrance—Dolly was muharrassed, and. she slipped throutrh the curtains and the folding door into the back room. Presently she heard Claude's step on the stairs. and he went out to meet him.

" Visitors," she whispered. " Lady rosbrooke, I believe. I was just finishing dusting when they came in upon me---and. then I slipped. away. Of course, they had no idea who I was.' " Oh," wli;ii3red Claude in return. better conic in 110 W tald be introduced."
" You hat

" No, no, Claude," said she hurriedly. "Not now, dear , it'm not dressed. Besides this is only a business call, and you've no right to bother about introducing your wife,—not this time." " Perhaps not," said Claude. " All right. We'll leave it, then." So he went on into the front room, and Dolly re. turned to the back room.

Dolly sat down and waited for the momentous in- terview to pass. She heard voices, but made out no- thing that was said. After the first few sentences of greeting, the talk flowed on without interruption and almost without pause, Claude's voice perform- ing a full third. Dolly was glad that he seemed to be getting on so well with such desirable clients, but when the talk became frequently rippled with laugh- ter and still continued without hint of ceasing, she began to think that the conversation was more pro- tracted and entertaining than business demanded. Then she told herself that the time seemed long to her because she was doing nothing, and she set her- self to accomplish some drawing. Still the conversa- tion flowed and rippled on, and Dolly paused to won- der if the ladies would have stayed so long, or been SO ready to be interested and amused, if they had known that the poor artist's wife was in the next room. She considered the matter :—Would it really discount Clande's chances of advancement if it were generally known that he was married Would it seriously damage the prospect of a remunerative commission if Lady Fosbrooke knew that the person in the print dress and white apron who had received her was the young artist's wife 1' Dolly believed that it would ; she could search out no strong reas- ons for her belief, but she felt certain upon instinct that her belief was right. It hurt her very much to believe so, but with characteristic resolution she pressed her belief to her bosom. Anon the ladies rose to go, and Claude conducted them down to the door. He returned and burst in upon Dolly, radiant, excited. " Hooray !" he cried, seizing her hands. " settled that I'm to paint her portrait ! ling to-morrow." " You took a long time to settle it," said Dolly. " Did we ?" said Claude simply. " Alt, but we Were talking of many other things. Charming, in- telligent ladies they are both of them—especially Miss Fosbrooke. Pity you were not in with us, Dolly." " Do you think, Claude," she asked, " that it would have been as nice—that they would have 10un4 it as nice—if I had been with you t" " Nicer, Dolly, nicer, of course. But you mu.st be introduced to-morrow.': _

" I think not, Claude.: We must remember, my dear, that this is a purely business engagement with you : a man doesn't introduce his wife to all his business clients, nor do they expect her to be in- troduced."

" Oh, but this is different, Dolly. Hang it ! I'm not a man in the City !" " No, Claude," said his wife. " But you are just a sort of tradesman, with something to bell that you want somebody to buy." " It's not like you, observed Claude, somewhat .wistfully, to say nasty things of that kind." " Perhaps not, Claude, darling:" said she, " and I'm sorry if I've hurt you." She drew herself closer to him. " I've only been thinking that in business matters we should be business-like--at /east, that I should."

"Do you mean that Lady Fosbrooke and her daughter would not take any notice of us if it were not for the portrait-painting ?" asked Claude. " I mean that we—or, at least, I—should not ex- pect them to. It is likely enough, and proper enough. however, that they should be interested in the artist— in you—without caring to know anything about the artist's people—his wife, for instance,—me. So, Claude dear, I'll remain in the back room to-mor- row, please." " All right, Dolly," said Claude, with a light turn of the hand, "have your way. After all, the thing is to get the portrait begun and done, and t,o earn the two hundred pounds.".

"Two hundred ?" said Dolly. "Is that what they offered? How glrid lam for you, my dear." " Yes," said Clau-do, " a very nice sum for a be- ginner—isn't it. Didn't I mention it before Yes, my own dear," continued he, embracing her, " we'll be able to set up house on it." " Ah, Claude," said she, " let us not be rash let us stick to business, and remember that two hun- dred pounds won't come to us every day." " We'll get hung, my dear," said Claude, "in the Academy, and that will bring us ware re- quests for portraits, and more sums bigger, per- haps, than two hundred." To Doily belonged the last word. " Let us wait," she repeated, " and kliek tvo nest"

div.head: BRITAIN 'AMONG THE NATIONS.
div.p: BRITAIN 'AMONG THE NATIONS.
[By Mr. H. :Whitham.]
Quite a nuraber of qusstions arise in one's mind while perusing the daily paper, and the trouble is that these questions cannot be answered entirely to one's satisfaction.

Just now the States are a little amused over the question recently put in the House of Commons touching the attitude taken by Great Britain in the Spanish-American war. It seems .to be assumed here that the nations of Europe are pretty well calling over each other in their anxiety to prove to the States that they never, at any time, had any wish to interfere in any way with what America might think it right to do, or not do, with the Spanish-Cuban question. While the leading journal of the West treats, in a humorous way, the whole question it none the less points to the persistent attempt to make it appear that the United States would not have been permitted to deal with Spain as she did if Great Eritain had not given her consent, and says "in the interests of humanity this must be stopped." The writer goes on to say—" It will cease when it is made perfectly clear, ati it is sure to be, sooner or later, that Great Britain was the nation which most actively mooted projects ef interference with our course in dealing with the Cuban affair." This little play of hide and seek among the nations may not be of much importance and nothing tragic will re- sult from it but none the less it answers at least one question, and that question is the title of a book now before me,— "WRY AMERICANS DISLIKE ENGLAND" Leeving the question and the book for future notice,it is enough to say that the native American, as well as the imported article, read it and believe it, the same as they read and believe the school book which tells the school children that the I politics of the States and of Great Britain will bear no comparison, the latter being so very corrupt. Turning our attention to another matter that I seems to find plenty of work for the telegraph operators, but of which, I must confess, I see little notice taken of in the English papers I receive, Mr Chamberlain seems to be bent upon deserving the remark that was recently made of of him : Mr Chamberlain is an excellent tool—very sharp and of first class temper, Unfortunately he is a tool with- out a handle." I know Mr Chamberlain,having met him on trade union matters more than once with the result that I have little respect for his honesty of purpose, but even the devil most have his due, and therefore I applaud his famous Edin- burgh speech. Those who remember the Franco- German war and the conditions under which the peace agreement was signed will stand by Mr Chamberlain now that he is assailed for answering in a mild yet forceful manner his unreasoning critics. To refresh the memory I give the portion to which Germans take offence, " I think the time has come, or is coming, when measures of greater severity may be necessary; and if that time comes we can find precedents for anything we do in the actions of these nations who now criticise our barbarity ' and cruelty,' but whose example in Poland, in the Caucasus, in Algeria, in Tonqain and in the Franco-German war we have never ap- proached." Where is the man who can deny the truth of these simple words? If such an one exists let him study once more the whole of the Polish question and he will knew the German for all that he shows himself as a bully at home, and, as the I Americans say, a bull-dozer abroad. Herr Somer- lburgh,an anti-semitic Radical,a man whose radical- ism helps him to become a Jaw-baiter could in the ' German parliament class the British Army as a " mob of thieves and robbers, unfit to he compared with the glorious Germans." There may be something more in this than is seen on the sarface. Count Von Buelow wiping his feet on the British uniform may think it the best way of keeping Mr Chamberlain popular, and so leave him with plenty of time to look after other irons that are in the fire. Germany's emperor has now sat on his throne twenty years. He has bad no great war on his bands, as every one expected he soon would have. His record stands at fair in that respect, but he has other, and not less important matters to attend to. The industrial situation is one that gives him and his ministers trouble. To me, he seems to bek in a dilemma as to what course to pursue with the American invasion,end so,while his grey matter is considerably•disturbed, he sends an order to America for the building of a yacht, and manages it so that the President's daughter I shall perform the christening ceremony and his brother visit the Sta,es. England is supposed to be watching all this with great interest and concern. Germany has great interests in South America. She would like to be able to turn one or two of its republics into German Colonies, but the Monroe Doctrine stands in the way, and Uncle Sam is too big a fellow to quarrel with. The next five years will be full of tremendous events. The characteristics of the various nationalities are an interesting study. I have associated with pretty nearly all who want something more, as a garment, than a tall hat and a celluloid collar and I have no hesitation in saving that the German leads all, even my own countryman, in stupid ignorant brutality. Not long since a German officer in an article that was published in essay form stated that he could with 96,000 men cut the great arteries of exportation, and so paralyze the industrial and commercial life of the United States. This Baron Von Edelshein with his wonderful knowledge of America's resources calculated that not more than 20,000 men could be opposed to him, and these would be armed with old stye muzzle-loader Rune, Now if this rubbish had been given out by an English officer all'the world would" have wondered. English insularity, and the bovine character of the people would have made many a text. It is no use calling names, the German is what the military system of the nation has made him. In the untravelled Englishman there is a certain con- ceit that seems born of tradition, just now, in two especial features war and commerce, this is being knocked out of him. With the German it is very different. During the present reign he has had peace, and the present Emperor inherited all the enthusiasm that could follow a glorious victory, ef which there are details it seems impossible to refer to. In industrial pursuits the German found him- self in an entirely new field. True, Germany may be looked upon as almost the birth place of the purely industrial classes, hut the dominance of the military casts forbad anything like the growth of the mill and factory system which the discovery of the power of steam developed in England. A power- ful, and almost the only reason that can be given for Encland's growth next to her industrial energy has been her ability to colonize. In these latter years she has seen the wisdom of placing her colonies on a free and independent footing, and in not a few instances have the colonies felt as if disinherited, and :have behaved accordingly. No'favoureds cation' clause gave the mother country undee pre- ference over Other nations. and it is, to-day, only England's ability that will get new markets to enable her to keep those she already has. The German looks at the matter from a different stand- point. Jealousy and ambition fill hisfehreaet. Neither the Foreign!Pecretary's mileespeech,nor his doings ll in South Africa would have been noticed had the mills and factories of Germany been doing a booming trade, but with these, to a large extent shut down, socialism extending with leaps and bounds, protection neither snaking trade, nor keep- ing wages above the starvation point, conscription ruining the proepeete of her manhood, why this jealousy and ambition had to take some active shape. England has seen alittle of it, in my opinion America much more. The Germans muet be coddled. Some short time ago a couple of German professors holding their professerships in American universities thought fit-to take their vacation in the fatherland and what they sew and heard they have described. The desire to colonies:its a growineeand practical feel- ing withvthe German. He fails to see that, so far, lie hits signally failed in this Looking to Australia "he saw he would have to break Great Britain'e supremacy as a sea-powenbefore he could drenm of conquering Australia." South Arn?rica on the other hand is composed of quite a number of weak and impotent states which Germany /laird-it overpower without any difficulty. No thought here of the Monroe Doctrine, The German of to-day thinks with Bistnark that, the Monroe Doctrine is only a bit of American Impudence In an unpronoun able German paper appeared the following ce- " Thoee Germans could only be saved, if they had the good sense to unite in adjoining settlements , to form tone or more German states within the' Union, and to secure thus as one solid body politi- cal influence and preserve their nationality. There is nothing in the constitution of the United States that is in the way of such an undertaking, nor are they lacking the room. As soon as a leader were found, the work would become Possible." I think it will be allowed this is rather tall talk, and when our German professors pointed to the folly of the whole business they were invited

to write an occasional article on American affairp "provided I would write in the satirical so pleas- ing to the German reader." The professor, German , bear in mind, and in his native land, says :—" How often we had to hear what hypocrites the Ameri- cans were, and how they could not begin to be com- pared with the Germans in point ef character, magnanimity, bravery and warlike qualities." However jealous, and vindictive Germany may be in her attitude towards England, she is much more so, but in an undertone, towards the United States. Her strong feeling against England is the outcome ot the latter nation' refusal to be a party to hostile action towards the States. The closing words of an article published in a German paper immediately after the fall of Santiago proves this,—" Yet there may come a time when the advantage ofla continen- tal European concert, based on the idea of I righteousness pure and simple, will, too late be ! recognised when the humiliation of Spanish 'pelf respect will prove injurious to the lself respect of Europe. And what will, in the end, prevent the Yankee, power-swollen as he now is, from stopping short tat the boundary of Canada ? England ought to consider that." The discussion now going on as to England's attitude during the Spanish-American war is interesting when viewed in the light of what the Germans had to say at the time. The Keilnis:he rolksseitung of July 13, 1819, had this to say: "If it should come to a Anal over- throw of Spain as a colonial power, and all events seem to point to that, England will bare this result on her conscience." Let England get clear of the horrid work she has on hand in South Africa, she may heal herself of the cuts, and the blood that has run through using the "knife without a handle,' and certain am I that she will see in any attempt' made by the continental powers to force a struggle with Americeonly humane reasons,and policy to go in hand with the American nation. A German writer says: "We must not he unmindful of the ominous fact that the United States may be and in all probability is that power with which Germany will fight for life and death." England's hope just now lies in the clearance of Downing-street. HENRY WHITHAIT, 1318, Guerrero-street, S.F.

div.head: CAUSE OF RAILWAY ACCIDENTS.
div.p: CAUSE OF RAILWAY ACCIDENTS.
Manchester Driver's Views.

In the agitation for shorter hours of continuoua duty for railway servants the strongest point that can be urged in support of the teen's claim is consideration for the safety of the travelling public. Flow many cf the railway accidents that occur in Great Britain in a year are due to the excessive strain under which railway- men constantly labour? The majority, no doubt, are traceable to this cause. We find very often that dis- asters orise not through want of rest, but through the heavy strain which engine-drivers, signalmen, and in fact, railwaymen of all descriptions have to undergo at the holiday periods of the year, when traffic is heaviest.- AR a former engine-driver aptly put it tea Manchester "Daily Dispatch" reporter. "A. man bas'to be in the pink of condition to bold any rail- way post safely." Mr Edwin Tingley, the speaker, now landlord of the Nelson Inn, Pickston-street, Hartaurhey, Manchester. was until recently an engine-driver on the Midland Railway, and knows whereof be sacaks. "I've been at an engine's throttle for 300 miles in a stretch," he continued. " so I know what severe strain there is in the work. But I held my own well until four or five years ago. when I had three severe attacks of influenza in succession, and I thought I would feel the weakness for the rest of my life until I was put on my feet by Dr Williams' pink pills for pale people. The first attack completaly prostrated me, and when the attack was over I felt as wenk as a child. In fact, I was literally broken up. There was a weakness in my eyes, and it always seemed as if black spots were floating before them, I was left also with a palpitation of the heart, and my limbs were stiff, especially about the ankles, and at various times I was unable to put my boots on. In short, I felt a wreck. What influenza leaves in its train is worse than the disease itself. " Yes," he resumed, in answer to a further question, " I was able to work after an interval of five or six weeks, but I was absolutely miserable, and nothing was a pleasure. The following spring I had a return of the disease, and the effects were similar, and again after- wards I had a third attack. As I have said, I was just able to work, but the strain wag terrible. Sometimes I was taken to be drunk. I felt so queerly. " Doctors," be continued, " attended me, and did everything in their power, but I did not feel that I was making progress. But one day,aftet I had been rendered helpless by the dreadful disease for a third time, I read in a paper about a man who had been cursi by taking Dr Williams' pink pills for pale people. It was a similar case to mine. My daughter also brought me a book,and there also I read of another man having been cured who was similarly afflicted. At last I determined to try these pills. I taok one box without feeling much effect but when I was part way through the second I noticed a distinct improvement. This induced met° continue, the treatment, snd I am glad to say that after taking six boxes I was completely cured. I first noticed that the weakness was becoming less, and in time that I was actually gaining strength, The palpitation of the heart ceased to bother me, and my appetite improved. When the six boxes were finished I considered that I was as strong and well as lever was in my life." " And was there no return of the malady 2" asked the reporter. _ _

" No. Last spring, when it usually broke out before, I had no symptoms of it, and I feel so well now that I am confidently looking forward to escaping again this spring. am only too delighted to give my testimony as to the benefit I derived from taking Dr. Williams' pink pills. I regard them as the best in the world ; and I never lose an opportunity of recommending them to my customers whenever an opportunity presents itself."
Mr. Tingley, it may be added, looked the picture of health,.

The long prognosticated split between Lord nosebery and Sir Henry Campbell-Bannerman (and their respective sections of the Liberal Party) has come at last, and, as is often the case with long expected and constantly delayed events, it came with -remarkable suddenness in the end. It was immediately caused by Sir Henry Campbell-Bannerman's speech at Leicester, in which he denied that the Liberal Party had cleaned their slate of Home Rule, and asked whether the ex-Premier spoke from within the tabernacle of the party proper or from a vantage. point outside saying that he had put practicallS the same question a month before, but had received no specific answer. This Lord Rosebery read in his morning paper in Berkerley Square the day after, and replied to by rqturn of post in his now famous letter. apologising. for his obtuseness in not having grasped C.-B.'s crystallised challenge, and declaring oefinite separation. His two reasons were 0; olifference of their views on the War and the question 'of Home Rule, as now understood. In favour of this final and irrevocable split politicians of all shades and con- ditions of opinion have this to say, that it clears the air and lets everybody know how and where they stand, and it *ill force all individuals, in or out of the Rouse of Commons, to decide under whose banner they will range themselves. For Lord Rosebery's letter forecasted no hanging up of his arms and return to the obscurity of privacy or the lone furrow of independence, but sounded a distinct note of leadership, and stated that he was no longer in solitude. Both at Chesterfield and at Liverpool his lordship gave forth an apologia for his political life without suggesting that he proposed to lead, using the speeches rather as thermometers with which to test his position and popularity. To this he has had a certain response which shows him that he is not alone in his points of difference from Sir Henry Campbell-Bannerman and the more Radical section of the party. As a result, " C.-B." threw down the glove at Leicester, and the Earl as promptly picked it up, and now, it rests with the Liberals to , settle each for him- self which master he ' will serve. 'Then will come the tug of war for supremacy between them, as any prospect of a reconciliation between Rosebery and Campbell-Bannerman looks , as hopeless as between Harcourt and the former or Chamberlain and the Liberals. Such is the present state of affairs, and we stand at the cross-roads of a political crisis as surely as we did in 1885-86, and the result thereof cannot at present even be oonjectured.

If his Holiness Pope Leo XIII. is spared another year, the occasion will be one memorable not only in the annals of Roman Catholicism. but also in the modern history of Europe, as he, who has always been celebrated as a ruler of upright pur- pose, purity of motive and desire for the universal weal, will celebrate his silver jubilee. He is, how. ever, very old, and at times feF,,ble, being over ninety years of age, so that great anxiety is often felt for his health, but he alone shows and feels no fear for himself, discharging his many duties as com- petently and conscientiously as her late Majesty 'Queen Victoria. These two great rulers, heads of opposite Churches ae they were, had the greatest mutual regard for each other, and it was generally , understood that the death of his great and lonoured contemporary Ii felt by the
HIS HOLINESS POPE LEO XIII.

WHO WILL CELEBRATE HIS SILVER 41.71311EE NEXT YEIR. Pope. Not only is next year the silver jubilee of his headship of the Roman Catholic Church, to which he was appointed on February 20th, 1878, but it is at the same time his golden jubilee as a Cardinal, ms he was proclaimed by Pope Pins IX. in the Consistory of December 19th, 1853, and, further, - the diamond jubilee of his episcopacy, as he - , was preconised Archbishop of Daimetta by Pope Gregory XVI. on January 27th, 1843, and con. uecrated on February 19th. From this it will be seen that, if he lives, 1903 will indeed see the summit of a great career which ranks amongst the finest of modern reigning potentates. The position of Pope is probably the most influential for good or bad of any in Europe' and apart from religious differences of opinion. his steward- ship of this great and historic office must be pronounced by the unprejudiced student of modern 'times to have been filled without fear or favour in the interests of right and peace. The question •of a fitting. successor to Pope Leo XIII., when the occasion arises, is no easy one for many reasons, but it is expected that Cardinal Ilanapolls, who, it is understood, is the successor favoured by the present Pepe himself, is the most likely .eandidate for the headship of the Church of ~ Rome. But it is hoped that the day of selection will be postponed for some time, though it can hardly be many years under the circumstances.

This week Paris has been taking i! self FOlllO - what seriously over the centenary of the birth ..of Victor Hugo, who first saw the light on the 26th of February, 1802, in the French c,pitai, which, therefore, naturally led the eelebrations, which were echoed in Brussels. Guernsey and 'other places inti- mately connected with the life of the great roman- ticist and poet. The whole of Paris was more or Jess decked with bunting, while the day was public holiday, and at night there were il- luminations. A statue by M. Barrias was un- veiled on the Place Victor .Hugo, and in the Pantheon there was an enor- mous official re- ception, at which poems were recited and speeches delivered in his honour. M. Gabriel Hanotaux, formerly Minister of Foreign Affairs, was chosen to speak on behalf of the Trench Academy, and the fllllCtioll was at- tended by the President of the Republic, the members of the Government, the representatives of Victor Hugo's family, and live hundred invited

pestle ',presenting all branches of art, while Vier* was accommodation for five or six thousand others throughout the enormous building. From the roof of the Pantheon was suspended an enormous crown of gilded laurel leaves, and tk. whole church was hung with blue velvet, embroidered with the same design in gold thread and the monogram " V.H." The house in the Place des Vosges, in which he lived from 1833 to 1848, was opened as a Victor Hugo Museum, and in the evening his celebrated play, Les Burgrares, was given at the ComiAie Francaise. M. Leygues, Minister of Public Instruction' ordered the pro- fessors of all the lycees in France to lecture upon this national idol and all his works, and three thousand pounds have been voted for the distribution of a commemorative medal, struck in honour of the day. His place in literature can be better defined since his death in 1885, and possibly he was more of a personality than a great literary influence. The French , consider him their greatest poet, and he was the picturesque figurehead of a generation in their world of letters; but his prose came rather as the close of an epoch than the initiation of a new one. Directly descended from Chateaubriand, he was the last of the romanticists' and after him came the new school, founded by Balzac' his great contemporary, and elaborated by Flaubert and Zola, which has had a far more lasting effect on the pre- sent age. Apart from this altogether, Victor Hugo has two great claims on English sympathy— much of his best work was written on British soil, and he was practically the first French critic to insist upon Shakespeare's greatness.

The Premiership of Spain may be a high and honourable office, but it is certainly no bed of, rests, and Senor Sagasta, the present Prime Minister of that distressful country is the least • envied of men. The long strain of the rebellion in Cuba and the unfortunate war with tha United States which followed, have had their natural sequence in the desperate state of Spanish finance. Since peace was made there have been some signs of recuperation in the Peninsula, but the nation's recovery is made difficult by the Ministerial un- rest which seems chronic at Madrid, even though the Cabi- net is not dis- placed by any of its rivals. As a consequence dis- affection is rife throughout the country, and the gravity of the seditious agitatioa which has broken out recently is sufficiently illus- trated by the proposal to place the whole kingdom under martial law. The general strike which has so mysteriously paralysed Barcelona threatens to spread, and there is evidence of a highly-organised conspiracy, based on an alarmingly wide foundation of popular discontent. It is feared that Don Carlos may be behind the malcontents, and this is not at all improbable, as the rumours of an impending Carlist rising, which are Always in the air, have latterly become more definite. It may well be that the Pretender contemplates striking a blow for the throne before the coming of age of the young Spanish King, Alfonso XIII., on May 17th next. It will, therefore, be seen that the seriousness of the crisis demands great firmness on the part of Senor Sagasta, and vigorous action by the Government of which he is the head if order is to be promptly restored in the Peninsula.

The entries for the twenty-third Show of the Shire Horse Society held this week at the Agricul- tural Hall, Islington, show in the most satisfactory way that the breedinc, of Shire a is yearly becoming more popular With British farmers. This year the total of 860 entries is the largest on record, exceed- ing by 1.93, the big muster of twelve months ago, and by 214 the number exhibited in 1890. This gratifying increase is probably Partly due to the entries of owners who have young animals' to sell, and find the Agricultural Hall a good market. The spirited demand and the general average.of the 215 animals sold by auction at the last show no doubt encouraged breeders to send all they could spare, not so much in every case witk
SKETCHES AT THE SHIRE HORSE SHOW.

the hope of winning a rosette as in receiving a satisfactory cheque on sale day. There is an ever-widening field for the noble shire to fill, and in all likelihood many of the splendid animals who have appeared in the ring this week will find their way to South Africa, to be followed by numerous others of their kind very shortly, The Shire Horse Society was incorporated in 1878 "to improve and, promote the breed of the shire or old English breed of cart horses, and be the means of distribut- ing sound and healthy sires throughout the country." In furtherance of these objects the SOblety, which numbers three thopsand members, has issued twenty - three volumes of its Stud Book, containing thousands of pedigrees, while it has now held twenty - three annual shows, at which prizes representing a value of upwards of £20,000 have been awarded. An this and other useful work is carried on by the Society by means of the subscriptions of its members. Its operations are of national impor- tance, and in almost any other country would devolve upon the State, if, indeed, they were under- taken at all. The Society. affords an admirable example of the British application of the principle of self-help, and, happily, landowners and tenant farmers alike have given it their heartiest support. The Shire Horse Show; like the Whit-Monday Cart i Horse Parade and the Cattle Show, s popular with. Londoners, and they help to swell the daily ceow4 0 visitors very appreciably.

Mr Longehaw did not approach them until October or November of 1901, after ' the work had been done. The specifications were approved and signed in August, 1900, and notices were seat out by the Town Clerk stating that they would be open for inspection et the office of the Borough Surveyor for a specified time. Was it not idle to ask the magis- trates to believe that the Borough Surveyer bad refused an inspection of the sprcifications ? Apart train this, the magistrates had to say whether there had been an unreasonable departure frxn WI hppeifications. The Corporation contracted with a contractor, and it was to their interest, for they had to maintain streets alts - wards, as well as to the interests of the ratepayers, that the work should .be properly carried out. Counsel pro- Iceeded to read the specifications and showed that it differed anaterially from what Mr Long9haw presumed It to be.

Thomas Longdin, borough surveyor, gave evidence in support. He said he hod no recollection of seeing Mr Longshavi in 1900, and be certainly did not refuse him or any other person an inspection of the specifications. Reproduced the signed specification for the work dated August, 1909, and bearing a signature of Robert Heaton. Mr Acton (after examin ng it) said there was no stamp on it. Witnesa (continuing) said be advised the contractor to use cinders in preference to red rock sand, as in wet weather cinders made a better job. The proportion of Rawtenetall setts used was 85 per cent. The excava- tion averaged about 12 inches. The concrete was 4! inches in some places and 3 Inches in 6thcm It was impossible to get a uniform depth of four inches. Dia experience taught him that the concrete hardened with age, and it made a very solid bed when mixed with clinker. Re was perfectly satisfied with the work. Mr Acton : Do you suggest that Mr Longshaw did not make a nom, ni your lithographed specification ? Witness: I don't remember him making a copy. Mr Acton: You have heard him swear that ho came to your office and copied the printed spnification ? Witness : I never saw him at the office befo • the final apportionment had been made.

Mr Acton : Can you suggest any reason why Mr Long- thaw should take the trouble t) copy the specification without his attention bad been called to it. Did you tell him it was the crdinary printed specification ? Witness : Certainly not ; I nersr remember seaing him there.

Mr Tobin admitted that there was a conflict cf evi- dence. He sugeeeted that Mr Longsha w bad made a copy of a portion of some contractor', bill of quantities and not of the sp2cificatons. Herbert Flatton, assistant bcrouch surveyor, said he did nct see Mr Longshaw at the Borough Surveyor's office until November last year.—Croas-oxamia.d by Mr Acton: He was not the assistant surveyor in 1900. Mr Seteliffe occupied that position in 1900. _ Mr Acton conceded that there bad been no departure . _

from the specifications produced. The queetion was whether Mr Longehaw wee ehown the specifications upon which be based hie calculation. Mr Tobin said the specifications were deposited for month, If by some mischance Mr Longshavr did not see them or copied something else, tbat was his own look-out.

Mr Acton said he did not propose to waste the time of the Court by contesting the case further if Mr Tobin's specifications were accepted by the magistrates as hay- ing been the specifications shown to them or which they night have a3en.

ihe Magistrates retired, and on returning into court, The Chairman said they had no reason to doubt that these were original specifications. Mr Long. thaw must unfortunately have copied from a wrong document. If ho did not see the sped- ficationa be might have done, as they were advertised, he supposed, in the usual way. Mr cton pointed out that the objection was genu- inely raised and under the circumstances it would be a terrible hardship if poor people were called upon to pay heavy expenses whilst investigating matters which they bad a perfect right to bring before the Court. The Chairman, after a short deliberation of the magistrates in private.said the magistrates did not wish to give!the impression that they were putting down any reasonable objection on the part of any of the in- habitants, and they had decided to ask each party to pay their own costs.

div.head: :THE MAKING OF PRIVATE STREETS IN ',WARRINGTON.
div.p: :THE MAKING OF PRIVATE STREETS IN ',WARRINGTON.

Objection to the Apportionment. Considerable interest was taken by property owners in Warrington in a case which was heard in the Borough Police Court on Tuesday morning. A special court was held for the purpose of hearing and determining the matter of objections to the final appertionment by the Corporation of the cost to be paid by property ovr nem for thetnaking of certain streets and passages in the boroug6. The magistrates were Mr Birched (who pre- sided), Dr Fox, and Messrs J W Hayward, and H

Thornton. Alderman Sutton, Fair°lough, Shaw Green, and Hutchinson, and Councillor Smethurst were else on the Bench, but did not adjudicate. Mr Tobin, instructed by the Town Clerk (Mr J Lyon Whittle), appeared for the Cornoration,and the objectors were represented by Mr Acton, instructed by Mr Long- too. Mr Browne watched the proceedings in the interest of Mr F J Bennie, the contractor for the making of the streets la question. !OPENING STATEMENTS BY COUNSEL. Mr Tobin in opening the case, said the Corporation had executed what was called private streets work under the Act of 1892. When the contract was made the estimated expenditure was provisionally apportioned among the,/ people whose houses abutted upon the proposed works or whose houses would receive any ' special benefit from the works. The work was carried out, and the Borough Surveyor made in accordance with the Act a final apportionment of the expense. Toe final and the provisional apportionment differed because in some cases the actual expenses were a little less and in other cases a little more than was estimated. The final apportionment having been made, the different owners were entitled if they thought fit to raise objec- tions to the apportionment. Some four owners had raised such objections. Under a particular section of the Act they might raise three objections. They had raised two, ono tnat the apportionment was not made in accordance with the section, and the other that .there had been an unreasonable departure from the specifica- tions, plans and sections. Having raised these objec- tions it was for his friend Mr Acton to support the objections and give to the magistrates his reasons for asking them to deal with them. Mr Acton submitted that that was not so. The pro- ceedings were the earn° as though the Corporation were proceeding summarily against the objectors to force payment. The result was that Mr Tobin should call evidence to prove that the provisional apportionment was made in accordanceiveith the statute, then that the work was done, and afterwards that the final apportion- ment was in accordance with the statute. Then it would be for hi en (Mr Acton) to call evidence in support of his objections. Mr Tobin laidi he was not suing for the money, If he was Ise would have to prove every step from the beginning to the end. The magistrates were there to deal with his friend's objections. It was only aommon sense that his friend should state his objections, so that the Corporation might give their answer to them. The magistrates agreed. Mr Acton said his first objection was that the direc- tions of the Act were not carried out at all. Mr Charles Longshaw' who was the chief objector in this case, celled at the Borough Surveyor's otlice in November, 1900, with a view to seeing tie specifications, plans and sections in accordance with the Act. Nothing of the kind was forthcoming. Mr Longshaw, who was con- corned to the extent of something like £l4O, found that there was nothing at the office except the ordinary ordnance nap, which was no guide to him, and so far from there being special specifications in compliance with the Act there was nothing except the ordinary general specifications which were applicable, he under- stood, to all kinds of street making and contained only the vaguest information as to the way in which the woek,was to be carried out Mr Tobin submitted that his friend could not go into that matter. Assuming what Mr Acton had said about this gentleman going to the Borough Surveyoi 's office was correct, it had nothing to do with the inquiry they were now conducting. If there load been something wrong with the provisional apportionment it was for Mr Loneeshaw to make objection within a month from the provisional apportionment being made. Mr Acton said he was not pointing to this with a view to attacking the provisional apportionment. He men- tioned it to introduce a conversation Mr Longsbaw had with the Borough Surveyor. In answer to Me Longshaw the Surveyor said that ceetsin things were to be carried out and certain materials used, and he (Mr Acton) was going to prove that that work was not done. The Borough Surveyor told Mr Longshaw, in addition to drawing his attention to an extract from the general printed form of specification, what would be the depths of the excavations. Mr Longshaw had been in the street malsiog business himself and was an expert, and was therefore well qualified to judge about what was told him by the Borough Surveyor. The Borough Surveyor toll him . .
the depth of the excavations in Ba ck fiostock-street ___.. . . . .

would be 16 inches, in Bostock-street North 16 inches, in Bostock-street South 12 inches and in Green-street yard and passage 16 inches. Upon what he was told Mr Longshaw calculated that he was going to be fairly charged.Wlt turned out, however, that the excavations were something absardedly less than what he had been told. In Back Cartwright-street, the excavation instead of being 16 inches was 12 inches ; in Bostock-street north, the excavations were Tor 8 inches ; in Rostock- atteet South, 6 inches and in Green-street, 12 inches. Mr Longshaw had been told by the Surveyor that the setts to be used were to be Raivteostall setts, and the jest of the materials in accordance with the printed form which he copied. ELECTION OF TREkSIIIIER. SOME INTERESTING REMINISCENCES.

Councillor PIEIPOINT proposed tne re-election of Mr NV 11 Robins m as treasurer, and referred in complimen- tary terms to that gentleman's services. Mt J DEWHIMST seeonded, and the resolution was unanimously agreed to. Mr Ronineorr thanked the members and undertook to continue the duties of the office for another 12 months. Continuing he said that at about the time of his Appointment as treasurer a little ever forty years ago,the club ground was in a very pleasant spot,—Bank Park. The late Mr Crosfield paid for the professional. Mr Thomas Litton paid the rent, and a few other gentle- men bought bats and balls when they were required, , Trouble seemed to come when the Volunteers were enroll- ed about 1859. The Greenalls and several other promin- ent players left them to join the Volunteer movement, and about the same time the old supporters felt that they ought to be relieved from their resp insibility of paying for rent, tackleoka. Accordingly they all tried to make the club self-supporting. In this they succeeded , very well and their next undertaking was to increase : the size of the ground, which cost a great deal. A tsar : or two later the Cheshire Lines Railway came and push- ed them a bit further away, adding further cost to make a fresh ground. They still got along very nicely, although always in debt, until the ground was absorbed by the Park, when they were forced to move to their present ground. Their landlord, Lord Winmarleigh was very good in letting them have the ground and at the same time gave them £5O towards putting the same in order. Many members of the club might remember what this field was like. They had to build a (-mall pavilion or dressing room and to fence the field on two or three sides. The first pavilion cost about £2OO and the present pavilion which was subsequently erected cost £777 so that the two buildings incurred an expense of £l,OOO. The fencing and laying of the ground with bowling greens ko,loaa also cost a good deal of money, but the debt was now happily cleared away and they were enjoying what they had been labouring and struggling for for many years. During many years in their eariy lease of the present ground they were not favoured with such an energetic committee as they had at the present time, so that the trouble was all the greater for the few who stuck to the ''work, Since the bowling greens were formed tney had had compara- tively little trouble in getting an increased revenue which had assisted them very materially, until at the present time the club stood possessed of everything on the premises, with nothing further required from the members but to enjoy themselves and keep up the stan- dard which had been maintained and which, he con- sidered, rel!eted great credit on bath the Committee and members, generally.

div.head: Tortured by Sciatica.
div.p: Tortured by Sciatica.

" Lila: a red hot wire pressed through your leg from the hip to the foot, ' is the vivid description of sciatica given by Mr. Charles L. Maddeaux, of 53, Northcote Road, Walthamstow Essex. He should know, too, for he has suffered as greatly as any man could. Mr. Maddeaux holds the respon- sible position of electrical superintendant on the "Argonaut," that splendid steam yacht of the Co-operative Cruising Co., Ltd. "I was under three doctors," he told a Sun reporter, "one of them attending me for eighteen months, but in spite of their skill I .continued to suffer. Recovery seemed hopeless. For years I was unable to dress myself. To attempt to put on my socks or my shoes myself was ridiculous. I could not bend from the hips, and if I tried the pains became terrible. " At last I was induced by way of an experiment to take Dr. Williams Pink Pills. The effect was marvellous. I had taken the pills for two days only when I found the stiffness already going out of the hip, and I was soon able to stoop sufficiently to pull on my boot. Within a fortnight I was practically cured. The pain had ceased entirely after I had taken one box. This was followed by freedom of the use of the joints, and then by the complete recovery of the use of the leg. Within a month I was able to go about my work again, and have ever since been a new man, active, free from pain, and in excellent health. " Two years after Dr. Williams' Pink Pills had first cured me, I met with an accident—had my foot and leg twisted. Sciatica set in again. I took Dr. Williams' Pink Pills. In a few days they cured the sciatica again, and from that day to this I have never had the slightest sign of it."

div.p: Knows What Rheurnatisrtn ts.

Ms. THOMAS EUNSON, of Newcastle, knows what rheumatism is in its severest form. He is an engineer, living at 16, Malighan Street, South Benwell, and he gave the following particulars to a Newcastle reporter : " I had been an invalid for over a year. I was seized with bronchitis, and that was followed by rheumatism and sciatica. A doctor attended me. but eventually gave me to understand that the complaint was chronic. I gradually lost the use of my limbs and could not stand. The pains I suffered were terrible, and I was never free. The slightest movement aggravated the rheu- matism, and made horrible twinges in my joints. Of course, my general health became very poor. I was not inclined to eat, and the long confinement made me nervous and despondent. Some years previously I had taken for a slight attack of the same complaint Dr. Williams Pink Pills for Pale People, which did me a great deal of good. I decided to give them another trial. I went to Yorkshire for a month, but had to be carried to and from the train. However, I soon found that Dr. Williams' Pink Pills were doing me much good, the pains gradually disappearing, and after a month's experience of them I was able to walk a little, and gradually there had come a welcome recovery." " Now, sir," he continued, "I am sixty next birthday, and after suffering like that, I can now do two miles walking without assistance. I feel something of a young mart again. • I have had no other mediolue but Dr. Williams' Pink Pills since July last year." His good wife willingly corroborated the state- ment, saying that the change in her husband's condition was little short of a miracle.

div.head: WARRINGTON CRICKET CLUB.
div.p: WARRINGTON CRICKET CLUB.
Annual Meeting. --- Formation of a League Decided Upon.

There was a large attendance at the annual meeting of the Warrington Cricket Club which was held at the Patten At(ll3 tiotel on Thursday last week under the presidency of Mr William Richardson (president). A SATISFACTORY BALANCE SHEET. .

Toe balance sheet was submitted and showed that the income amounted to £417 8s 31 and the expehses to £403 4i Li, leaving a balance in hand of £l4 45 2J. In moving the adoption of the balance sheet, the CHAIRMAN said it was with pleasure that he moved the adoption of the balance sheet last year, on account of the prograss they had made in reducing the debit balance, and he expreased the hr:pe that when it was moaed this yesr the deficit would not only be wiped off. but there would be a balance on the right side. That hope had been realized, and for the first time for many years the balance sheet contaiaed that welcome phrase " balance in hand" to the amount of £l44s 2J. When he said that at the end of 1898 the club was £ll6 18i to the bad, he thought they might indeed congratulate themselves, and he hoped it would be a long tune before they receded from that satisfactory position. After dealing with several items of expendi- ture Mr Richardson referred with pleasure to the fact that toe gate money for the season was an increase upon the previous year oi £l3 5s 91, being £34 93 10d. This was an important improvement and he hoped it would continue. He was sure the House committee deserved the thanks of the club for their good management. The sports were not SO successful fluan- cally as they were lair, year. There were other meetings on the same date, which no doubt made a considerable difference, but the balance from the fireworks display more than made up for it. The atuouat received for obscriptious was £9 133 61 less than the previous year and the remedy in tus opiaion lay with the members, Be hoped every one would consider it his duty to encour- age his friends to join the club. In looking forward to the coming season, diem appeared t a him Co be one or two matters which would have to be attended to which would necessitate ecoceny as much as possible. Ile thought the next committee would be obliged to take in hand the paintitig and repairing of the psvilion which would probsbly mean a considerable item in the expenditure. Moreover they might not again renew the letting of the football ground from which they received £2l. ifoweser,be thought they might commence again with confidence and be hoped they ahould have a pleas- ant and succassful Reason. Councillor W YIERFOINT seconded and the motion was unanimoasly agreed to. F.HIMATION OF A LEAGUE PROPOSED.

Some discussion took place as to the advisability of forming a cricket league for she district. Coancillor TINNION was very much in favour of the propose, as he thought that if a league were formed it wouid aroll9B much more interest in the work of the Club. • Dr SMITE{ was of the opinion that the suggestion if carried our would lead to cricket in Warrington becom- ing more enthusiastic, and large gates would be attrac- tod to the matches, For the last few years cricket had been at a very 1)w ebb in VVarrington as regarded the 1 enthusiasm and gates, and few matches had been woo. Mr E A CONNOR a,nd Mr J W Hussy also strongly advo- cated the formation of a league. Eventually the SECRETARY (Mr C H Unsworth) moved the following resolution : That it be an instructinn to tbe Committee from this meeting to consider, and if thought advisable, to take such steps as they may con- sider requisite tor the purpose of forming a cricket league in this district." Dr SMITE{ seconded, and the rasolution 's as carried unanimoualy.

ELECTION OF PRE,IDENT. The CHAIRMAN proposed the election of Mr Reginald Silcock as president of the club, remarking that that gentleman was qualified to fill the position. He had been connected witla the club for many years and had always given hi 3 hearty support to every scheme which had been brought forward to further ths interests of the club. Mr R T Fairclough seconded and said that Mr Sil- cock had dune ail in his power to further the interests of the club in all its departments. He was sure Mr Silcock would be the right man in the right place. The resolution was carried with acclamation. Mr SILCOCIE then took the chair and made a short speech, thanking the members for his election. He said tie felt proud to become their President, and con- sidered his election not only an honour, but an evidence of the good feeling which existed towards him. Lord Rosebery, in one of the addresses which be delivered at Liverpool said the greatest pr as a man could have in this life was the triend,hip and cordiality of his fellow subjects and cicizens, and he (the speaker) thought none lof those pressnt would dispuze that statement. Cou- tinuing,the speaker said he felt his election was an henour that he really was not worthy of, but he would do his best to fulfil the office as well as fie could, and, if he received the sympathy and goodwill of all the members of the club every task would be easy and all difficulties would be removed. One thing that made the pesitioa difficult to till was that Mt Richardson was a very difficult man to follow. He had taken a very lively and personal interest in everything that appertained to the welfare of the club,and:tiad identified himsell with every scheme wshh had had for its object the maintenance of the good feeling which bad existed among the members. He -(the speaker) hoped that he might be able to emulate Mr Richardson's good example and that at the end of his term of office the club would be in as pros- • perous and healthy condition as it was at present.
