div.head: WAS THE HAY MUSTY?
div.p: WAS THE HAY MUSTY?
Dispute at the Warrington County
Court.

Before His Honour,Judge Bowen Rowlands, K. C at the Warrington County Court on Thursday last William Winstanley, farmer, Stretton, sued Dania Donnellan, horse dealer, Fairfield House, Manches- ter-road Warrington, for ..-05 43, the value of 1 ton 6 cwts. of bay supplied.—Mr Fowler represented the plaintiff and Mr Steel, the defendant. Mr Fowier said the defendant had paid £3 into Court and the dispute was as to the quality of the hay. William Vs instanley, farmer. Stretton, stated that he toed supplied various firms in Warrington with hay. In June last year he received a letur from Messrs Buckley's manager (Mr Muskett) asking him to acrid a load of hay to Buckley's and another load to the defendant. Nothing was mentioned about the quality of the hay. The price was £4 per. ton. He supplied the hay which was good sound clover hay and the first complaint he had ever received respecting it was from the defendant who wrote him on the 25th Septemher.—ln cross examination by Mr Steel, witness said he was not aware that Mr Muskett, the foreman for Messrs Buckley, had promised to get the defendant " good prime bay." Mr Steel, in answer to His Honour, said the defend- ant on the day following the delivery, found on opening the trusses that the hay was musty. He complained to Mr Muskett, who agreed to take some of it back again. Defendant dealt with Mr Musket%and did not know the plaintiff at all. Evidence as to the good quality of the hay was given by Henry Winstanley. son of the plaintiff who carted the hay te defendant's premises and said that defend- ant helped to unload it and did not complain about the quality of the hay. William Perrin, traveller for the Warrington Slate Company, said he delivered the bill for the hay supplied by plaintiff to the defendant. Defen- dant made no complaint whatever about the hay. On witness delivering a second bill a short time afterwards Idefendant said he wished to see Mr Winstanley as two or three trusses of the hay were not " up to the mark." Alfred Lord, foreman carter at Messrs Buckley's and Patrick Monaghan, horackeeper for the same firm, also gave evidence. For the defence Mr Steel said his client's story was that Mr Muskett, the manager for Messrs Buckley and Company, had been to the habit of pur- chasing hay for the defendant at various times. In Jule, 1951, defendant met Mr Muskett, who asked if he could do with some good hay, After considering the matter for a few days defendant said he could do with from a ton to 25cwt. of I hay, but as his horses were high-class animals it must 'be good. There must be no top or bottom trusses, and no musty bay.. He understood that Mr Muskett was I acting as agent for some farmer, and gave him the orthr. When the hay was delivered young Winstanley said it was good stuff and there was no"- must" in it. Defendant did not then notice that there was anything the matter with the hay. On opening one or two trusses the next morning he found the bay was musty. He complained to Mr Mu3kett who took back 84 cwts and offered to accept £4 for the remaiecler. Defendant,how- ever, refused to pay more than £3. 11)r Muskett was called and said t3e ordered the hay at the request of the defendant, who was passing Messrs Buckley's establishment and saw some hay from Mr Wzustanley's beiug unloided. Witness was not an agent for Mr Winstanlev. kefendant did cot make any com- plaint about the hay antil three months afterwards. On hearing this evidence, Mr Steel decided not to proceed furt6er with the case, and his Honour gave judgment for the plaictiff with costs.

div.p: for an. alternative Ministry is postponed by the events of last week. But the cynics are pr3mature in suggesting that Liberalism has thereby been hopelessly ship- wrecked. The separation may much more reasonably be compared to the breaking away of quicksilver, where the two circles formed in the process have not lost their essential characteristics by the action. It is due to Lord ROSEEERY to bear that in mind, because when the Unionist Press is not rejoicing at the Liberal upheaval, it is endeav- ouring to make him the victim of its eulogy by its exuberant approval of his course. The Liberal party was purged of its Conservative leavening when the DUKE of DEVONSHIRE and his Whig friends bade it farewell, and those who have chosen to be I known by the good old name of Liberal since and to share its adversities are not likely to go over to the Government side now. The criticism w`iich the CECIL administration is receiving from its own supporters, and its inability to rise to the require- ments of the people, put any rapprochement o that sort out of the question.

In the course of the next few days the people who have been accustomed to take their leading from Liberal front benches will be crystallising their opinions on the event of last week, and the best advice that members of Parliament can have and newspaper writers can give them is to remain_ ber that this is after all a family matter in their discussions in clubs and their homes. They should- be careful lest they lay the emphasis on the things that are transient and overlook the many points of common sympathy. Lord ROSEBERY and Sir HENRY CAMPBELL-BANNERMAN have set an ex- ample to their admirers by the avoidance of any words that should seem to be discourteous or harsh. When a group of extremists at the mass meeting of London Liberals at St James's Hall treated the name of Lord ROSEBERY with scant courtesy Sir HENRY CAMPBELL-RANNERMAN set himself with determination to secure for Lord R3SEBEICY'S views a sympathetic attention. That happy dis- play of generosity finds its counterpart in Lord ROSEBERY'S cordial recognition in his letter of C.-B.'s services to the Liberal party at a time of unusual difficulty. His letter might have been conceived in a different spirit, having regard to the warm recognition of his services at Chester- field and Liverpool. In both instances there is the same clear desire that when the history of this matter comes to be written what is said now shall not assist the enemy to blaspheme. Let Liberals emulate Lord ROSEBERY and Sir HENRY in reso- lute avoidance of bitterness ; and let them remem- ber that the differences which have produced this division are not profound or vital. Mr. GEORGE WHITELEY took a philosophic view when he insisted that measures should have the first con- sideration and not men.

The Rev H. B. Blogg, vicar of Frodsham, is en- titled to some sympathy, as well as the criticism which he has been undergoing for the past few days. Mr. Blogg has been delivering an address on "Sunday observance," and ia the course of his remarks he made a well-meant endeavour to show how the English Sunday might be brightened and, in his opinion, bettered. It is unquestionably true that boys would be better playing football or cricket on Sunday afternoon than "loafing about smoking unhealthy, pernicious cigarettes." Thus far the vicar trod upon safe ground, but when he calmly suggested that football, cricket, golf and the like might be indulged in upon the Sabbath— after service of course—he got himself into a morass which he will find some difficulty in escap- ing from. The continental Sunday is not the "worn-out old bogey" he alludes to, but a very real and objectionable misuse of the Lord's Day. To encourage the passion for open air and exercise, with due regard to church worship,was permissible and even praiseworthy, but here the rev gentle- man should have stopped. All boys do not smoke " pernicious cigarettes," and we presume the Sun- day sports would not be confined to those who did. Consequently, if Mr Blogg's suggestion found favour we should have the usually peaceful Sunday afternoon given over to the excitement and noise of Saturday,\ with results which might benefit physically but would do no good mentally or morally. It is as imperative that the Englishman should look upon Sunday as Sunday, and not merely as a day which affords unique opportunities for personal pleasure. No doubt the Rev H B Blogg would admit this readily. We wonder if he can really have thought what would be the out- come of such. "Sunday observance" as he courageously but unwisely advocated?

Mr. Henley, on reading a; advertisement of his "Hawthorn and Lavender" in American periodi- cals, will be interested to learn that he is " un- doubtedly England's greatest living poet." For the moment, perhaps, he will think fame has given him his due. Then will come tile reflection that this is the little way of the American publisher I with a book to sell. What has Mr. Swinburne 'done? the ordinary reader may ask; to say nothing of our Poet Laureate, whom ,they are in- clined to think rather a deal of in America; of Mr Meredith, of William Watson—nay, even of Stephen Phillips. In the same way Mr. Farness is announced as "without question the world's leading caricaturist." Well, on this side of the Atlantic, as thorough admirers of Mr. Furness's great talent, we are still con- strained to admit there are others. Hardly less laudatory is the announcement that E. Nes- bit's "Would-be Goods" "ranks with the best work of St3venson. But one of the best of these puffs-preliminary is that mentioned by a writer in the Literary Supplement of the "Times." A pub- lisher declares a novelist to be "as good an example as need be of the writer whose aim is literary and not commercial." The retort is obvious that the publishers are as good an example as anybody can wish of the publishers whose aim is commercial and not literary. There are bright examples of the contrary method, as the writer suggests, such as Mr. W. C. Brownell, who, as author and pub- lisher too, keeps the departments of business and literature in proper relation to each other. But to one who prizes the dignity of letters the adver- tisement sheet of an American literary papers are generally painful reading.

----- The decision of the Conference of Friendly Societies on the subject of Old Age Pensions is certainly a step towards the settlement of this difficult and complicated question So much must be admitted, even by those who see grave objec- tions to the plan adopted by the delegates. The great point is that .Mr Chamberlain asked the Friendly Societies to take the subject in hand and 'submit a scheme. They have done so, and it is bound, therefore, to have favourable consideration from the most powerful Minister of the Crown. He may not approve all that the delegates propose, but it is clearly incumbent upon him to declare with how much he does agtee, and where he differs from the authors of these proposals. This will undoubtedly mean progress. Some impatient souls point to the example of the Colonies, where the subject of Old Age Pensions gives little difficulty, and are inclined to taunt our statesmen and our legislature with lack of feeling or lack of courage, because they will not rush at a solution of the problem on the lines laid down by the Trade-Union Conference, and give universal pen- sions to the veterans of industry. Mr. Chaplin's Committee, however, starting with the very best intentions, found it impossible to agree upon a scheme, so obvious were the objections to each one raised. The great fault of the Friendly Societies' proposals is the inquisitorial power it places in the hands of the pension authority, who are to try a man for providence or improvidence when it is

div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
FEBRUARY 28ra 1902.
The Contract THE Commoners who Scandals. gathered so numerously in

the House of Lords on Mon- day evening on the off chance of a sensation were rewarded by an object lesson which they will do well to lay to heart. They came no doubt with their minds imbued with the thought of Liberal separation, and they saw the Opposition in the Lords working together in perfect unanimity from the front Opposition bench and the cross bench. Any stranger who followed Mr. BALFOUR'S advice, and did not read the daily newspapers, could have made but one comment, and that was how cohesive wee the Liberal elements in the Upper Chamber. Lord ROSEBERY followed L 3rd TWEEDMOUTTI'S lead as if party leadership were a matter of no consideration, or, if considered, it should be on the maxim in honour preferring one another. Several Liberal peers spoke giving a delightful example of amity and co- operation, and it is difficult to see why the same plan should not be applied in both Houses to other questions of the day. There are enough of them on which there is substantial agreement to give the Opposition plenty of work. Of course Lord TWEEDMOUTH'S motion was defeated. But faced as the Opposition is by huge majorities in both Houses, the benefit of these debates must be for the future rather than for the present. Lord TWEEDMOUTH brought together with accumulated force the strong rumours which are prevalent as to scandals in regard to War Office contracts. If these are gross exaggerations, as the Government assert, there should be no reason for refusing a vindication of the persons concerned and for assuaging public anxiet J. The Government pro- fess that to grant an inquiry now would paralyse operations in the field. They overlook the 11 fact that they granted inquiries as to the concentration camps, which proceedin gs were carried through smoothly and with beneficial results. The proposal to allow these contract scandals to be reviewed when the war is over is an obvious evasion. People are so heartily tired of the war that, as Lord ROSEBERY said, they will be glad to forget at the earliest moment. We will all be so jubilant when peace is restored that no one will think of the contract scandals. The lessons that might be obtained now will not be learned then. The suggestion that no one at the War Office could be relieved of his duties for a few hours while he answered ques- tions is absurd on the face of it. Lord MORLEY, who spoke rather severely about Lord ROSEBEBY, agreed that a prima-facie case for inquiry had been made out; but argued that it was undesir- able that it should be made now. If the inquiry extended into the whole conduct of the war there would be some reason in this attitude. Since, however, the inquiry asked for is only in rbgard tothe remount purchases and the meat contract, the attitude is utterly unreasonable. The net effect of the debate is to leave on the public mind the impression that there have been scandals, and that the Government are determined that they shall not be inquired into until the Greek Kalend s.

IT is to be doubted rhe Duty of Liberals. whether the Unionist Press i 3 serving the Government to the best advantage in its glee over the troubles in the Liberal party. There can be nothing morejcalculated to arouse the differing elements to a sense of the absurdity of the present situation. The workers in the country are, by Unionist jibes, brought to reflect that Liberalism does not depend for its existence either on Sir HENRY CAMPBELL-BANNERMAN or on Lord ROSE- BERY. Measures not men is the old and ever-new Liberal formula. The importance of the personal element cannot be ignored, and the prospects that Liberals might offer to the country the material

gap.desc: skipped/gap: fewer than 20 non-control characters after cleanup

div.p: quite impossible that all the circumstances should be before them. But if the public will not endure this, still less would they endure the charge of maintaining the idle and the dissolute. These two difficulties are the lions in the path. Will Mr. Chamberlain, or any other leader, now be able to poiat out a safe way between them?

Lord Rosebery's "definite separation" from official Liberalism may or may not be an epoch- making event in political history but it is cer- tainly an occurrence of the deepest significance. Failing to agree with the present Liberal leader on some vital principles, the noble Lord has suddenly given up the attempt to do so, and thus brought to a crisis the differences on the war and Home Rule which are to be found among Liberals. Sir Henry Camp- bell-Bannerman is certainly left in possession ef the field, but Lord Rosebery seems confident of being able to gather followers under his own banner. Whether he will succeed is the all-im- portant question just now. He has many admirers but we are inclined to think that his reputation for words rather than deeds will bamper Lord Rosebery in any endeavour he may make to or- ganise a party professing the new Liberalism.

2A Provincial Letter.

No such good fortune as yet A London corres- pondent of a leading provincial paper gave promin- ence on Monday to a rumour that had been circulated on the Continent and on the London Stock Exchange to the effect that General Botha had entered into negotiations with Lord Milner for surrender. Students of the financial columns of the paper referred to, and of other journals, would observe on the following day, after the somewhat serious decline South African Stocks, following the speculative purchases of a fortnight previously,that these securities advanced on the strength of the rumour in question. No doubt many sales were effected, and it is perhaps not unduly cynical ta suggest that when this was done the object of the said rumour was fully accomplished. Anyhow,the Colonial Secretary, in reply to a question on the subject in the House of Commons on Tuesday even- ing, ssid he had received no communication as to the offer of Botha to Lord Milner to surrender on certain conditions. Far any little disappointment that may have been experienced by too credulous readers on this point, however, there was authentic news to offer of the capture or surrender of some noted rebels, and authority for believing that an- other combined attack is in progress against De Wets force,

It is a long time since one saw so formidable a list of distinguished invalids as the morning Papers have presented during the past week. The Rouse of Commons would appear to be a very hot— bed for the propagation of influenza. Mr Balfour isjsuffering from his third attack, and among others Who are in the clutehPs of "la grippe '' is Mr Walter Long, the President of the Local Govern- ment Board. The reason for the present spread of influenza, which is by no means confined to the House of Commons, or to London. but is reported from all parts of the country, is not easy to deter- mine. There ara those who claim to speak with authority in saving that the close atmosphere is mainly responsible, and the possibilities, at any rate, are that the humid atmosphere, together with a temperature high for February, coming so soon after a spell of cold weather, has rendered the human system more susceptible to the operations of the influenza bacillus. The epidemic, as it may now be called, is not even confined to England, it. appears; for the Continent is again under the bane- full spelt, and the greater number of patients, there as here, seem to be persons of "distinction." Of course, this classification may be more apparent than real, because:the ailments of the rank and file are not usually recorded in the public press.

When the Bishop of Hereford obtained his Select Committee to inquire into the Prevalence of Betting and the best means of preventing it, there was a general disposition to treat the matter lightly, and t.,? predict that there would be no practical results. "alit the bearing of evidence before the Committee and recent revelations in connection with the Liver- Pool bank frauds have produced quite a change in the publietone. Witness after witness of unim- peachable authority has testified before the Com- mittee to the deplorable con.equences of street- betting, to the development of the practice within the last few years among those who can leant afford to indulge in it,and to its extension even to WOM3O; SO that many persons previously indifferent about the matter have become impressed with the urgent need for action Arising out of the remarkable bank frauds alluded to, the possibilitY of a man in a com- paratively humble position engaging in betting t ansactions, one of which involved .a sum of no - . _

less than:Xls,ooo,is one in regard to which advocates of reform in the Betting awl Gambling Act 3 are now having much to say. The Select Committee will scarcely ignore the lessons enforced by the Liverpool case. It has long been recognised that the Acts in question are in a somewhat chaotic con- dition, that they do not afford sufficient guarantees tor the honest operator, and that they have _
opened the door widely to the fraudulent. But those who called for their amendment were con-

fronted by difficulties and limitations, the nature of which will be obvious to those who possess even a superficial knowledge of the subject. It appears, however, that the Liberal Bishop of Ifereford, find-

_ ing that he can now reckon among the supporters of Parliamentary intervention several Unionist member, of both Houses, is not without hope that the presentation of the committee's report may be followed by a proposal on the part of the Govern. meat to legislate on the subject of betting. It is admitted tnat nothing can be expected this session, but it is looked upon as certain that recommenda- tions of theicommittee, it they are not unanimous, Willyat be such as to command attention. The "Liberal Bishop of Hereford," it may be said in this letter, is one of those persons to whom re- Pose is a stranger, and one of his mans active efforts is being brought to bear upon the prevention of cruelty to wild animals. But it seems a "forlorn hope" that he will persuade the House of Lords to take his Bill, having that object in view, seriously. The Bill provides a penalty of £2O for the man who takes part or assists in the bunting, coursing, or shooting of say animal which has been kept in con- ' Anemnit, and is released for the purposes of "sport," and also for the man who keeps or uses, or assists in the management of any place kept for such purposes. It will be easily seen that the provisions are fairly comprehensive. Indeed, if they were to become law there would be no more shooting a; lluriingham—on existing con- ditions—and no more coursing for the Waterlo3 (Sup! These are considerations which in the Upper House, if not equally so in the Lower, would be - sufficient to Condemn the good Bishop's proposals. and prove fatal thereto.

r-3 The time has been When wooden " Nutmegs " were comm)n articles of commercq, and some of us have a vivid relollection of the fun and excite- e Went caused by the discovery of th fraud. But there is scarcely a world of difference between Wooden " nutmegs "and sawdust " tobacco." One however, came from across the Atlantic, which was Perhaps not surprising, while the other comes only from Ayant the Tweed," which ought to be a matter of wonder. In the latter case two enter- prising individuals,having been tried at Edinburgh at the instance of the Exchequer for defrauding the Inland Revenue,were theottter day fined the full Penalty of £2OO. From sawdust many useful things oaay be manufactured, but neither cigarettes nor snuff The frankness ot the accused persons appears to have been their own undoing ; for they' entered into communication with Messrs Wills, the Well-known tobacco firm, of Bristol, to whom they offered their spurious goods, with the result that they were "named to the Revenue authorities, "Powdered wood" was the design- ation employed, and with it they offered to meet Public demand for cigarettes and snuff. In this way does the ingenious ' eophisticator " continue to improve his opportunities, as if there had never been any serious attempt to amend the Food and Drugs Act. Tobacco it may be assumed, would be accounted a' drug" for the purposes of this prose- cution.

•Local authorities in various parts of the pro- l'inces can scarcely fail to be encouraged by the Parliamentary return, just issued, relating to Tramway Undertakings, where they have been con- sidering the advisableness of taking these concerns out of the hands of the companies. It appears that

outlof more than two hundred systems in operation there are only three that show any loss, and the loss even in these cases is too insignificant to be taken into serious consideration. Most of the undertakings, especially in populous districts,show very handsome profits, whether in the hands of local authorities or companies, notwithstanding the fact that few are wholly worked by electric or steam power.

It is not long since:ladies" pits and men's com- panions of the four-footed order were freed from the obnoxious muzzte,becaube it was supposed that rabies had been effectually " stamped out." But at Cardigan the other day a young fox-hound which was being trained for a local pack, went mad and bit several dogs, while many persons had narrow escapes.

div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.

DEPARTURE OF A RUNCORNIAN FOR SOUTH AFRICA. Mr A Clifford limmine, who has been enjoying a short holiday at home, sailed on Thurs- day last to Canetown on board the es. Suevic. White Star Line. He was one of,the first batch of Volunteers who left Runcorn over two years ago, for South Africa, and, after 12 months active ser- vice in the army, he accepted an appointment on the Imperial Military Railway at Pretoria to which he has returned. During his holidays at home he was presented with the active service medal and a silver watch, the latter being one of the six sub- scribed for by the townspeople of Runcorn. On several Sundays he has presided at the organ at the Parish Church,Saint Michael's and Holy Trinity Churches. Prior to his leavetaking a large party of his friends met at Rockfield, the residence of his parents, Mr and Mrs Charles A Timmins, to wish him God-speed and a prosperous journey. DEATH OF AN OLD RUNCORNIAN.

On Thursday evening last week there passed away at her residence, Chaucer-street, Mrs Ann Peacock, wife of Mr Ralph Peacock, one of the best known of the local preachers in connection with the Primitive Methodist body. Deceased,who was 74 years of age, was of a most kindly and generous nature, and on Sunday a large number of people assembled to pay a last tribute of respect to her memory, including Mr William Handley, Mr W Shaw (Mersey Mission- er),the Revs J Osborne and W A Eyre, Messrs J H Miller and C Sage, of Widnes, John Hayes, and the principal members of the denomination with which deceased was connected for so many years. The remains were cconveyed to their resting place by Messrs H Pilgrim,JlW flayes,S Booth and H Illidge. The principal mourners were: Mr Ralph Peacock (husband), John and Daniel Dutton (sons). G H Peacock (stepson), and a number of grandchildren. The service was conducted by the Rev W A Eyre; while prayer was also offered by the Rev J Osborne Mr J if Ivliller,and Mr C Sage. The favourite hymns of the deceased lady were sung during the funeral service.

div.head: FRODSHAM PUBLIC iN FINED.
div.p: FRODSHAM PUBLIC iN FINED.

On Wednesday at the Frodsham Petty Sessions hefore Messrs C Reynolds (in the chair) G Crosland Taylor and J Taylor, Harry Foster, licensee of the Cheshire Cheese Inn, was summoned far selling in- toxicating liquors GO drunken persons on his licensed premises on the 25th of January. Frederick Garner, Overton ; John Parker, Frodsham ; were summoned for being drunk on licensed premises.— Mr Giles, Chester,prosecuted on behalf of the police and Mr H N Linaker defended.—Sergeant Guilt stated he visited defendant's inn at 8 50 p and found the men inside the bar drunk with liquor be fore them. Witness called the attention of the licenses to their condition. Eventually the defendants were persuaded to go home. P C Proctor corroborated. for the defence a great number of witnesses were cued to prove that the men were sober enoughwhen they went home. The defendant said he was short- handed and his wife Could not go into the bar to serve. Defendant was fined 204 and 163 61 costs; Garner, 103 and 93 6d costs; and Parker 5s includ- ing costs. FUNERAL OF THE LATE CAPTAIN JOHN DA.VIES _ _ _

The remains of the late Captain John Davies, whose death took place at his residence in Bur- leigh-road, North Everton. Liverpool. on Thursday, the 20th February, were interred at Runcorn Ceme- tery on Monday afternoon. Deceased was a native of Runcorn, and had worked his way up to the position of master of the Cunard tender Skirmisher by characteristic pluck and perseverance. The Skir- misher is the steamer so much in evidence when Cunard liners are arriving and departing at Liver- pool. Deceased was familiar to thousanas of people who go on the Sloyne on Cunard visiting day (Friday), and he was held in high esteem by his employers, the public, and his subordinates. Captain Davies's ancestors have been connected with Runcorn for several genera- tions, in lithe iearly part of the:xixth century his grandfather was landlord of the Royal Hotel. During the war in the -.Crimea Captain Davies was on service in the Black Sea and in the course of his sea-taring career he witnessed many hair-breadth escapes ?and was the means of rescuing quite a large number of people when in imminent peril of drowning. He bore a jovial countenance,and was hale and vigorous look- ing almost up to the last. He caught a cold during the recent severe weather, and succumbed,as stated on the Thursday. He was 67 years of age, and leaves a widow and one child. Deceased was twice married. The funeral rites on Monday were attended by a large number of his colleagues and personal friends, and the remains were borne to their last resting place by the crew of the Skirmisher, in charge of Captain Faulkner, of the Satellite. The body was conveyed by rail, and the funeral procession was formed at the Runcorn station. Among those who preceded the hearse 11 were representatives of the Rose of Sharon Lodge (Runcorn) of the Grand United Order of Odd- fellows, viz. :—Messrs William Kirkham, Robert Wright, Captain R Hill, Captain 'Hadley, James Waring, Thomas Gilgrass, J W Bazley, E Jones, John Jackson, Tl, Ashcroft, T Bazlev, J Banner, John Thompson, James Waterworn, James Joyce,T Hancock, Captain George Heasley (marine superin- tendent Manchester Ship Canal, Runcorn section) Captain Dudley (marine superintendent, Earlam) Captain Ricsby. Ciptain H Hill, Captain Johnson Captain J Ellis (Runcorn), Captain Christie (Farnworth, Widnes,) Messrs W Shaw (sea- men's missioner, Runcorn), W Cooper Wid- nes), P 11 Matthews (Liverpool), Captains Bowger and Mercer (Widnes), Messrs T C Price, J Bebbington, W Cooper, D H Jones; W M Glen (chief steward, Cunard Company), L Bishop (band- master), J Corcoran (superintendent wharfinger), W Bankes, Ellis Low (Faxonia),A Adams, R B Brown, R Bell (Liverpool); It Owens (Wigan), W S Knowles (representing Mr J Knowles, Widnes), F L S (goods agent, Runcorn), S Hope (Hazlehursts Works, Runcorn), and others. The •coffin was draped with the Union Jack and the regalia of deceased as a member of the Rose of Sharon Lodge. The principal mourners, who occupied carriages in theirear, were :—Mrs Davies (widow), Mr T Davies (brother), Iklessrs G 11 Davies, John Davies and T Davies (nephews), Misses L and M Davies (nieces), Mrs G Davies, Mrs Jagger, Mr and Mrs J Banner, Mrs Corker (niece), Mr G Banner, Mr it Banner (nephews), Mrs J Ormes, Mrs Edwards, Mrs Mad- dock, and Misses Maddock. Notwithstanding the drizzling rain a considerable number of people turned out to witness the funeral obsequies of one well known to them as a Runcornian who had risen to a honourable position from humble circum- stances. The burial service was conducted by the Rev Bishop Baker, of Liverpool, and before the final scene at the graveside the hymn " Lead, kindly Light " was sung. A number of exquisite floral emblems were contributed by the deceased's family and friends.
SAD FATALITY TO A_ RUNCORN MAN..

On Monday a man named Schofield working on the " Cecil "lying at West Bank Dock, Widnes was engaged in emptying a bucket when he over- balanced and fell overboard. The tide was running strongly at the time and carried the man out in the , river where it was impossible to rescue him, and he was drowned. Schofield is a Runcorn man resid- ing in Surrey-street and leaves a wife and a large family. WIDNES MEN SENT TO PENAL SERVITUDE. At Liverpool Assizes, before lir Justice Bucknill, William Dunn, twenty-four, Arthur Foster, twenty- five, Thomas M'Grath, twenty-eight, and Richard Hughes, twenty-three, labourers, who had been out on bail, were charged with an assault on a woman, at Widnes, on January 19th. Mr Greer was for the prosecution, and Mr Rigby Swift and Mr Lord for the defence. The jury brought in a verdict of "Guilty." His- Lordship said the case was a bad one, and the sentence of the court would be seven years penal servitude for each prisoner. NARROW ESCAPE PROM DROWNING AT RUNCORN. Late on Saturday night a man named David Nevitt, residing (in Surrey-street, had a most unpleasant anti unexpected adventure when return- ing from Wigg's Works at the Old Quay. The night was rather dark, and owing to the slippery condi- ', Um of the footway Nevitt stumbled and fell into the Ship Canal. Attracted by his cries, a number of workmen were promptly on the scene, and after some little difficulty they succeeded in rescuing the man from what might otherwise have been a watery grave. Nevitt was removed home, and thanks to prompt and effective treatment he had on Monday completely recovered from the shock occasioned by his immersion. THETT BY YOUNG GIRLS AT WIDNES. . .

At Widnes on Thursday two youug girls named Mary Martin and Jane Dunn, aged eleven and thir- teen respectively,were charged with stealing Is 4il from Mrs Riley's shop, 71, Victoria-road on Monday last. They were also charged with stealing 6s, the property of Alice Draper, 88, Victoria road, on the 20th.—Police-cmstable Rutter apprehended the girls, who in answer to their respective charges, pleaaed guilty.—The Chairman characterised the offences as youthful depravity of the worst kind. He considered the parents much to blame for net lookitig properly after them,and bringing them up in the right way. They were bound over in £5 to come up for judgment if called upon. div.p: CUSTOMS AT RUNCORN.

The following is from the' Berwick Advertiser" of the 21st February :—Mr .1 H Harnil.on, collector of Customs at Berwick, who for twelve years was honorary secretary of the Runcorn branch of the Royal National Lifeboat Institution—an office he was obliged to resign on his promotion and removal to Berwick a few months ago—has been the re- cipient of an embellished testimonial, handsomely framei in gilt and oak, from the InAitution in London, bearing the signature of H.R.H. the l'rince of Wales, president; and other office bearers. viz , Sir Edward Birkbeck, Bart., vice-president ; and Mr Charles Dibdin, secretary. The wording of the testimonial ;is of follows :—At a meeting of the Committee of the Royal National Lifeboat Institu- tion for the preservation of lite from shipwreck, held at their offices, London, on the 13th day ot February, 1902, the following minute was ordered to be recorded on the books of the society, and to be communicated to J H Hamilton.Esq,—"Resolved that the best thanks of the Royal National Lifeboat Institution be pre&ented to J II Hamilton, Esq., in acknowledgment of his valuable co-operation dui. lug the period in which he occupied the office of honorary selretary of the Runcorn branch of the Institution."

div.head: RUNCORN NOTES.
div.p: RUNCORN NOTES.

[BY A COItRESPONDENT.I At the Rural Council meeting held on Tuesday Mr T Wright, Halton, proposed that the Council petition the Local Government Board to delete the clause in the Vaccination Act relating to the Con- scientious objector. It is worthy of note that the Council were unanimously in favour of the motion not a single councillor having the desire or the courage to splinter a lance in favour of the anti- vaccinator, S )eaking without prejudice it seems, on the face of it, decidedly unfair that a boly of men should force even a single individual to do that which his reason denounces as wrong. Without holding a brief for the anti-vaccinator does it not seem tyranny of the grossest kind that a person cannot be allowed to exercise his own discretion as to the advisability of having his child vaccinated? That liberty which public bodies clamour, as a rule, so loudly for themselves they should be prepared to give to others. The Council, like other public bodies,are frightened at the small-pox epidemic,aad obviously think that anything rather than nothing should be done to minimise the danger.

The Rev II B Blogg's utterances on Sunday obser- vance and the advocating of the Continental Sun. days have raised quite a hornet's nest around his ears. At present there is a very strong feeling on ofithe question in Frodsham district and all shades the community are oppo,ed to the idsaCof Sunday golf, football or cricket clubs.

Fishing is a sport which Runcornians have, for some time, taken very kindly to. Time was when the fishing members of the community could be counted on the fingers of one hand but now all this has been changed by the enthusiasm of one or two. The Runcorn fishing club inaugurated a few seasons ago, almost in fear and trembling, now commands the support ,of the greater portion of the anglers of the town. Latterly new changes in management to ensure its prosperity have taken place. Fresh fishing places have been hired and stocked with fish and it only requires the card of membership and an abundance of patience to win B:handsome prize'at the end of the season besides procuring well-stocked baskets of hook-caukhG fish.

div.head: , FOOTBALL.
div.p: , FOOTBALL.

On Saturday Runcorn travelled to Batley and smote the Yorkshiremea with unwonted vigour. It was not thought that the Linnets would render a good account of themselves but they happened to be in good form and fairly oatclassed their oppon- ents. The visiting backs played a far superior game to the home contingent and earned by sheer hard work the honours of the fray. Runcorn are now showing such good form that they should be easily able to beat Bradford whom they play on Saturday next.

div.head: WIDNES AND RUNCORN BRIDGE
div.p: WIDNES AND RUNCORN BRIDGE
COMPANY.

Annual Meeting. The third ordinary general meeting of the shareholders of the Widnes and Runcorn Bridge Company was held on Monday afternoon at the offices of the company, No. 6, Castle-street, Liverpool, Sir John Brunner (chairman of the directors) presiding. The report submitted was as follows :--" Daring the year contracts for the erection of the bridge nave been arranged, the foundation work being let to Messrs W Thornton and Sons, of Liverpool,and the superstructure being let to the Arrol's Bridge and Roof Company, Ltd., both being contractors of the higheit standing for work of this character. Although very little change is to be , seen at present on the site of the work, a large portion of the contractor's plant is on the site and good progress has been made in the preliminary arrange- ments and in the construction of the work at their works. Mr L H Chase, woo ham been appointed resident engineer, has taken an office in Runcorn, near the work. It is expected that the bridge will be completed about the middle of next year. The retiring directors are Sir John Brunner, Bart, M.P., and Mr LI Seton-K arr, M.P., both of whom are eligible and offer themselves for re-election. The auditor retiring by rotation is Mr Benjamin Cookson, who is also eligible for re-election." A balance sheet also submitted showed that the authorized and subscribed capital was £lOO,OOO, of which £20,000 (£2 on each share), had been called up, and £4lB 173 2. was due from sundry creditors. Among the disbursements it was shown that the Parlia- mentary proceedings cost £10,500 us Bd., whilst other disbursements totalled £3,775 OA 11d.,'.the balance being £6,143 43 7d. The Chairman, in proposing the report, remarked upon the commencement of the work and commented with satisfaction upon the condition of the undertaking. Mr H. Seton-Karr, M.P., seconded, and the report was adopted. Sir John Brunner and Mr Seen-Karr were afterwards unanimously re-elected directors, whilst Mr Benjamin Cookson was re-elected as joint auditor. A vote of thanks to the Chairman concluded the pro- ceedings.

div.head: Man's Ribs Broken.
div.p: A Man's Ribs Broken.

At Newton Petty Sessions, on Thursday, before Messrs T J Gillespie, Colonel Wood, and W Coiling- wood, Peter Williamson, of Vulcan Village,Newton, was charged with doing grievous bodily harm to James Winward, also of Vulcan Village. The in- jured man has been in Warrington Infirmary suffer- ing from four broken ribs, and appeared in court in a very weak condition. Complainant said that about twenty minutes to eleven on Saturday, the lith inst., he was going home whea he met Williamson and another man, who accosted him. Complainant went on home, and later on the de- fendant and the other man brought him out. A. struggle ensued, and while Winward was on the ground Williamson kicked Lim three timis, twice in the ribs and once in the face. He had since been in the Warrington Infirmary, and remained there for a week.
Cross-examinA, complainant denied that he kicked W illiamson first.

Evidence bearing out complainant's statement was given by James Molyneux, with whom com- plainant loiged, and lichael Coyne. Constable Schofield spoke to arresting Williamson at Burtonwood, at a quarter to five on Monday, 17th inst,and when charged with breaking his ribs, prisoner replied," Whit price him kicking me ?" For the defence prisoner said that when he was going home Winward challenged him to light. He pulled kis jacket off and a man named Robert Mackay, who was with prisoner at the time struggled with Winward. Williamson tried to separate them, and complainant kicked him. Williamson then kicked him back in the ribs. The bench bound defendant over to keep the '1 peace for six months in his own recognisance of .ClO

div.head: FRODSHAM RURAL DEANERY.
div.p: FRODSHAM RURAL DEANERY.
An Advocate of Sunday Sports.

The half-yearly conference was held on Tuesday afternoon in the Chapel-house, Runcorn. Toe Rev Canon Maitland Wood, Rural Dean, presided, and there was a good attendance. The Rev F G Slater, rector of Capenhurst, gave an address on " rho Provision of Clergy io P opulous Places," and said each new pariah had been each wed, but the ancient endowments had decreased enormously. Proceeding, he dealt with the Additional Curates' Society. There were he said five millions of people in England to day who lived practically as heathens, and three millions of them were in London. Taey would thus see that home missions were therefore necessary. In conclusion, the rev gentleman appeals] for funds,and said not cool v did the beneficed clergy of the country pro- vide one half 'of the assistant clergy of the Church, but they also were very much the majority of the subscribers of the Additional Curates' Society. He announced that the society would soon be compelled to reduce the grants made by 5 per cent. A discussion followed, during which the Ciiairmaa said there was a scarcity of young men for the minis- try, becaus i no clergyman could hope to make a for- tune. Even if he succeeded in becoming Archbishop of Canterbury he would not beg rich MAU ; he would still require private means to inset to any extent the great number of appeals made to him. He urged lay- men t) encourage their sons and others over whom they had influence to take holy orders, not for what they could get in a monetary sense, for no true servant of God would do his work on that basis. _

The Rev H B Blogg, vicar of:Frodshatn, de ivered an address on tt Sunday Observance," and said the clergy ought wit.' all t oeir might to make Sunday more bright and gladsome, especially for the young men and maidens and children. If Sunday was a dull and weari- some day they would probably grow up to hate it. They would naturally ask bow were they to make it a day of gladness ? Far the young he would say by encouraging them to play their games in the afternoon after Sunday school, football in winter, and cricket in summer. It might shock a good many worthy people t suggest such a thing, but surely it was better that our b•iya should be playing a healthy, manly game on Sunday aft .moon than loafing about smoking un- healthy, pernicious cigarett's. Older men, too, clerks. and others engaged in business, and kept in doors for most of the week, he would encourage to play golf on Sunday afternoon,provided they did not employ caddies and ale) most certainly on the understanding that they had observed the day as the Lord's day by attendance at mornirg service. He was also inclined to look with I favour on the practice of visiting relations and friends , on Sunday if it was after attending a service. Ho thought the clergy in that part of Cneshlre might combine to see that the men engaged in any works had freedom to attend a place of worship, if not every Sunday, at least , every altercate Sunday, so that it might be a day of I rest as well as of worship to them. There were cases in I Isis own parish wh,re men never had a chance of join- ing in any public wership. and he thought by combina- tion better distribution of labour might be arranged. He strongly sympathised with the passion for the open air, and he would welcome trippers to Overton Hills on Sun- flay if only he could be sure that they had first paid God the tribute of praise and thanksgiving which was His due. In order that these lovers of open air might have as much of it as possible he would close the public houses on Sunday, and thus avoid the rowdiness and the drunkenness which so often marred and destroyed the true enjoyment of the Lor l's day. Worship, rest, and vcreation should be the three main features of the Lord's day. Do not let the deny be afraid of introducing what was known as the Continental Sunday. That was a worn- out old bogey. which insular ignorance had too often conjured up. From what he had seen of the Continental Sunday he preferred it greatly to cur own. A discussion followed, but the ray gentleman received little support in his views except in the matter of Sun- day labour at works. Ultimately a committee was appointed to confer with the directors and managers of the works in the district.
The conference then concluded. INTERVIEW WITH THE REV, H. B. BLOGGI. AN IRATE VICAR .

A representative of the" Examiner" called upon the rev, gentleman to further elicit his Vows on the ques- tion of " Sunday observance." But though Mr Bing may be admitted to be the Cheshire champion of national pastimes, he cannotibe regarded as a past— master in the art of courtesy, for the humbld scribe was perforce compelled to admire the exterior only of his beautiful residence. As soon as the Vicar bad learned the nature of his visit^r's business he absolutely refused b be drawn into a further statement. Standing with the hall door ajar and with irritation marked on every feature he testily replied to a polite inquiry that he preferred not to commit himself in any way further than he had already done. He excused himself from detailing big views on the ground that big manuscript, which was the root of all the evil, was not in his possession. Asked whether he was prepared to establish or coun- tenance a Sunday football, golf, or cricket club, the rev gentleman replied with an emphatic " no." "The whole report" he continued, "is very much mutilated because only part of it has been giveu. I repeat Ido not want to9coremit myself and Ido not know why you want to write about it like this. It ie not necessary. It was simply a paper that I read." And the interviewer left the irate vicar's presence with the words ringing in his ears " the report is much mutilated." further interview with one of his prominent workers revealed that at one time the Vicar's grounds on a Sunday afternoon were thrown open with the idea of vetting people to church. Hs had never previously advanced such extreme views and their expression had I caused surprise and pain. At pre.ent Frodsham and district are in a state of ferment. The village itself has not taken kindly to the idea of the Continental Sanday. The dissenting minieters,the vicar's own churchworkera and even the man in the street are opposed to the in- movation of Sunday sports. And it is not too much to IMF that the Bev B B Blogg is in for a lively time for promalgating his almost Republican opinions.

The fcemightiv meeting ot this Council was held at Dutcon Workhouse on Tuesday under the presidency ot Mr S Woodward. RIVER POLLUTION AT HALTON. Mr Reginald Potts, clerk to tue Cheshire County Council, submitted cepy of report presented by the County Meiicsl Offic •r of Health to the Rivers Pollution Committee of that Council at its last meet- lag, and intimated that he was instructed to request that the Council would give effect to the sug- gestious as set out in the last paragraph of the report. The specified clause was to the following effect t—" The County Medical Officer of Health would sugeest that the Runcorn Rural District Council be pressed to con.

thane to take steps to stop the pollution previously reported, and especially that they give their prompt attention to removing pollution from Halton BrJok and Kingsley Brook." Toe Sanitary Inspector said that the Analyst commen- ted upon the brooks being: free from pollution. It was impossible to keep sewage matter out of streams.

The -Chairrns-ci said that if they allowed the sewage matter of the various properties to over- flow they did become a serious nuisance. It was a matter which required constant attention. The inspector had had instructions to attend to the matter aud he thought that the answer to the com- munication should be th a'. the matter has had and is still having and will have their beet attention. —,leliter further discussion,this answer was decided upon, the Clerk promising to bring the matter before the Halton Parochial C ommittee.

The Chairman : It seems to me that th proper course t 3 take is the one suggested by the Clerls. 3a the propisition of Ur it.ww...l it was eventually decided that this course be adooted.

THE SHIP CANAL SLUICES AT LATCHFORD. The secretary of the Odanchester Shin Canal Company wrote under date 14th February 1902, that the Com- missioners for the Coaservancy of the river Mersey had served upon the company an order to raise the caps of the sluices at Latchford locks to the height of 29 feet, 6 inches. The commissioners have power to enforce their order by mundamus or execute the work themselves. No decision has yet been arrived at by the directors but the height of the water in the Latchford pond is not governed by the height of the sluices at Latchford but by the weir at Woo!aeon which will not be eff,cted in any way by the operation of the order which toe com- missioners have issued.

Mr Swinton, surveyor. said he was of ooinion that they would not be afficted by t'le raising of the s uices. Mr Fs.rrington, inspector, pointed out th4t the only possible contingency might be the fl)ociing of the land.

VACCINATION. The Malvern Urban Di4rict Council forwar fad the following resolutions which had been passed by the Council and which it urged the Board to adopt.—" That this Council, as the sanitary authority for toe urban district of Malvern is strongly of opinion that in the interests of the public health clause 2 of the Vaccination Act should ha repaalad. Arai that the L ocil G oar aro- ment Board ghoul i be asked to urge the Government to introduce during the present session a bill dealing with efficient primary vaccination and re-vaccination The Clerk pointed out that Mr Wright bad a similar motion to propose and the two Lcould very well be con- sidared together. Mr Wright said that to a certain extent his motion had been forestalled by Lord Newton who hid made a gicilar motir in the House of Lords which had bean lost bv a majority of 20. On teat occasion the 1,-r i Chancellor told them that the wh,la of the officials con- nected with the law courts had to be vaccinated whether they liked it or not. Ha could not compal them but their services would not have been required unless they had submitted which wa ; certainly putting tho screw on them. At toe Stepney Hospital out of 32 nurses eight were not vaccinat ad and seven out of the eight contracted the diseaso while the others were not affected at all. He had pleasure in moving that section 2 relating to the conscientious clause be delered and that a copy of the resolution be sent to the Local Government Board. Mr Edwards seconded, enumerating the horrors nf small-1)1x, and contending that it was unfair that the mai lrity should be placed in danger by a few faddists. The motion was unanimously carried.

Mr Clad molt drew attention to the fact that over 37 houses in Weston had not had a supply of water for nearly a wr..ek, and that works had been also in the same condition. The Clerk rronfsel tint the matter should have his attention. This was all the business of public interest.

There were also present tho lt,w Canon Wood, Messrs F J Norman. W Handley, E Imison. Lightbutn (clerk), and A Lighttrurn (assistant clerk).

The recnnavnriatiOrl at:Termed. THE PUPIL TELCUERS' CENTRE.

The School Management Committee recommended that Mrs E Hawkins mistress of the pupil teachers centre: 09 allowed an increase of £lO making a total of £l2O per annum to date from lit March 1902. The committee further recommended that Miss Maria Rowlin son be appointed to awdst Mrs Ambler to exam,ne exercises at a salary of £lO per annum to commenc3 on March Ist 1902. Mr Handley in moving the adoption of the minutes said that the pupil teachers centre had not been in existence for 12 months. It; was the first organisation of the kind established in connection with the Board and they were careful at the outset not to alto w •the expenses to be of an extravagant nalure. It was then understood that the expenses should not permanently remain at the initial figures of 12 months ago. Already it bad been a greater success than .they had reason to
hope for in such a shnr: time. They had now some- thiug like 16 or 18 more pupil teachers drawn from the Board and the Voluntary Schools. of the town and neighbourhood. The voluntary schools . . . .

of course bore their proportionate and fair share of the I expenses. They began the second year with something like 28, which showed a very satisfactory increase. They believed that in their teacher, Mrs Hawkins they had one who had proved herself fully com- petent to fulfil her dufies. Not only was she competent In the sense of capability, but also in the interest which she took in the public teachers' gathering. She saw the advisability of even directing their studios outside what she was compelled to do by the terms under which she was appointed. From every point of view the centre bad been a satisfactory venture. Miss Rowlinson, the assistant mistress, examined the papers prepared during the week over which she spent a great deal of her time at night. They felt sun.) that in making this proposal they were doing what was right and reason- able, and they hoped the outcome would be greater effimency on the part of the staff. The whole of the Cost would not fall upon the Board, the Voluntary schools bore one half, and it was a singular thing that one half of the teachers came from the Voluntary and cn 3 half from the Board. Mr Norman seconded. He said it could hardly be regarded as an increase in the ordinary Remo of the term. If the number of pupil teachers increased it could not add much in the way of increasing the expenses of the Board. Not only did Mrs Hawkins direct the studies of the pupil teachers but he had heard of her taking them to ctaer classes in order to see that they were properly qualified for their profession. Already an important improvement had taken place which was to be welcomed as the pupil teachers filled an important part in the community. THE SCHOOL BOARD ASSOCIATION.
It as resolved ou -the motion of Messrs Handley and Norman that the Chairman and the Clerk attend the meeting of the School Board Association at London and that the clerk's expenses be paid.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS. RUGBY FOOTBALL.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS. RUGBY FOOTBALL.
By " Ovalist."

A few such games as that at Warrington between the honte team and Widnes would freeze off even the War- rington supporters —than whom I believe there are none more loyal. In fair weather or foul, during suc- cess and adversity, they turn up at the home matches with unfailing regularity. It takes a lot to daunt or disgust them, but even the Warrington spectator would hardly endure another such display as that of Saturday. Widnes are well in the running for the South-West Lancashire championship, and they came to Warring- ton fully convinced that they had small chance of winning, but quite determined to make a draw of the game by some means or other. And they suc- ceeded. Perhaps the feat will be recorded among the best that the Widnes club has achieved during a phenomenally successful season. To say that the crowd was disappointed with the display given does not half express the prevailing feeling.

After a month of idleness on Saturday they came down to Wilderspool thirsting for a keen struggle between the champions of one competition and a club playing in still higher circles. The game was certainly keen enough but the dull monotony and the utter absence of science made it a dreary exhibition to watch Right from the commencement the ‘Vidnesians took up the defensive and inaugurated a system of mark, punt, and rush which they stuck to for the rest of the game, even when they had the assistance of the wind. War • rington did at first open out the game and pass tha ball but eventually they fell, under the spell and were soon busily engaged returning the Widnes kicks and putting in fresh ones of their own. Any- thing more asinine could hardly be imagined. Warring- ton never could play tile kick and rush game, and for them to forsake their ordinary efficient style of play for the idiotic and lifeless tactics of the Widnes team was the height of absurdity. flow were they to score by punting, when the other side were slightly their superiors in that style of play ? Warrington are very much to blame for losing a valuable point on Saturday and to concede three points in one season to a second division club ought to bring the blush of shame to the , cheek of every member of the Warrington team. Though they are champions Widnes are undoubted second- raters, and on Saturday they played as such, judging football from the standpoint of science and skill. In one sense Widnes accomplished a good perform- ance,but to go on the field prepared to play for a draw is bad sportsmanship, and would soon end in the death of sport were it persisted in. One expects healthy rivalry and the desire to win to be the leading impulses of the footballer,and I am sorry the match on Saturday turned out to be such a miserable fiasco.

In one respect Warrington were unfortunate. Fish's absence counted for a lot, and lam sure that had he been on the team the game would not have been the scoreless, lifeless exhibition it was. Nevertheless Jones played exceedingly well in his place, and was very unlucky in having a fair try disallowed by .he referee after a great effort. Warrington do not seem to get on well with referees just now, and for some time past have had at least one try disallowed in every match they have played. Moreover recent suspensions have put the referees on their mettle, and they are very ready to think evil of an ordinarily vigorous tackle when a Warrington man happens to be the tackler. The players have itadeed to be careful to avoid suffering the fate of unlucky Burgess. Would that he had been on against Widnes.

Though they started well Allen and Edmonds made very little progress from the rear of the Warrington pack. Allen was always more of a defensive player, and Edmonds though he, did one or two smart and original things was not the success I had expected. I hope he will keep up his originality, and make up for lack of inches by the smartness which appears to be in him. I believe he can do much better than he did on Saturday. Talking of inches, Edmonds is not a Foulke by any means, and possesses the honour of being by far the smallest member of the Warrington team. When the ball came sailing towards him, one feared for the little un's complete annihilation, but he can field and pass in rare style —and these are good qualities.

The half back play on either side was poor, and that of the three•quarters not much better. Warrington did show a little better style than the Widnes quartette, but the centres were very much at fault in doing so much punting instead of playing the centre gains. Dickenson has of late developed a kick and run tendency which I hope he will drop at once, and return to the style of play which he formerly practised and which gamed him an excellent name as a promising three- quarter. Centres must play the centre game, and they cannot be too mindful of the fact. Widnes had an ad- vantage forward, the octet appearing to work harder than the Warrington lot, who do not follow up anything like as speedily as they used to do. At full back Irallam I and Tilley gave two fine displays and share the honours of the day for what good football there was. By the table below it will be seen that Warrington will have all their work cut out to keep ahead of •Widnes in this competition. It is true Warrington I have only two more matches to play, both with Wigan, but they will need to get four points from the colliers to be anything like safe. Widnes have to play Leigh twice, and Runcorn and Wigan away, so that their chances may be somewhat lessened in the future.
The Soutli•West Lancashire League table up-to•date is as follows : Point
P. W. P;r—A—rt,r. P. Warrington 8 ... 5 ... 2 ... 1 57 ... 37 Widnes 5 ... 4 ... 0 ... 1 ... ?.6 18 ... 9 Leigh Wigan 4 St. Helens

None of the Northern League matches were very ex- citing on Saturday, but it should be noted that Oldham again went down at home, Broadley and the Bradfordi- ans doing the trick. The burly Park Avenue captain is a valuable asset and no mistake ! Runcorn also did a smart thing in licking the cup-holders at Batley, while Salford undoubtedly met their masters at Swinton.

Warrington really seem to perforni better away from home than on their native soil. On Wednesday they journeyed to Fluddersfield with only small prospects of victory, but they defeated the Fartown men for the second time this season, by two tries to nil. Hudders- field have not won very many matches, but they have done well at home, and Warrington's performance was a smart one. The team gave a good all-round display and quite over-played the Huddersfield men in the second half,

Fish once more emphasised his inestimable value *to the club by scoring both tries, the first from a pass by Jones,and the second on his own after Deere had mulled the ball. The Huddersfield wing man got small chance of recovering himself,for Fish was on the ball in a flash and after beating the full back scored easily. No goals were kicked, and in this direction Warrington missed a few chances. Jones once more showed his capabili- ties in no uncertain way,and quite pleased the Hudders- fiekl folk, who remember him as a member of their own club. Dickenson also shaped better.

The match looked very much like ending in a draw for there was no score ten minutes from time. However Fish made no mistake about taking opportunities, and the result caused some woe in the Fartown district.

Another good performance was placed to the credit of Bradford on Wednesday, when they took down the Swinton "Lions "on their own enclosure by 8 points to 5 points. Consequently they resume second place iu the League.

Warrington have climbed a few places higher and now figure in the centre of the table, a position they are quite at home in. The clubs above have only a small lead, and with luck and good play Warrington should even yet finish in a creditable position. For several years Warrington have averaged a point per match and at present the scare is 22 points out of 22 matches.

Salford have been going strongly of late and the odds are that they will add Warrington's scalp to the num- ber they have recently annexed. To-day sees the first meeting this season between the New Barns contingent and Warrington. There is a chance of course that Warrington will rise to the occasion, but I rather think the superiority of the Reds at half back and forward, will gain them the points. There is a good chance however, for Warrington to distinguish themselves.
The Warrington captain, my readers will regret to bear is having trouble with his knee, and this week has
ME

been an inmate of Mr. Allison's famous Manchester establishment. Ile hopes to be sound again before the cup-ties start, and Warrington spectators will hope so too. Isherwood cannot be spared from the three-quarter line.

ST HELENS.
TERRIBLE DEATH AT S. HELENS.

At St Helene Town Hall on Monday, Mr Brighouse held tbe inquest on the body of Catherine Tatlock, aged twenty-two, of 21, Nythian-street, who died about noon on Saturday from burns received at her h-use on the 12:h inst. Patrick Morris, of 33, Wright-street, identified deceased as his dauguter. bee was the wife of Richard Tatlock, collier, but lived apart from her husband under an order of the magistrates. Deceased told him at the Providence Hospital that she was hang- ing clothes in front of tbe fire, when her clothing caught fire. Sarah Schofield said that On Ash Wednesday even- ing deceased came to her door and opened it. She was in flames, and said, " 0 i, missis, put me out, for I am turning to death." She got her husband's coat, and wrappedjit roand dei;eased,who in the struggle went out in the Meet a:raio. Witness shouted to the neighbours, and a man helped her to put out the dimes. At the time she took fire deceased had her baby in her arms, but put it down and ran out of the house.. The baby has since I died. It.was suffering from bronchitis at the time. The ury returned a verdict of " Accidental death." ST. HELENS DIVORCE SLTIT.—£3OO DAMAGES.

lathe Thyme s Court, on Wedoeaday, Sir F jetine granted a decree nisi to William Henry Boardman,stated to be employed at St Helens, on the ground of his wife's adultery with aMr Wardle, The parties were married in 1893, the petitioner then being a bandsman in the Lancasnire Regiment. thtunately he sold out and went to St Helens to work for his brother, the respondent staying with her mother in London, where she obtained employment at a hat faztory of which the co-respondent was manager. Ultimately she refused to return to her husband, and it was found she was living with the co— respondent. The jory assessed the damages against the co•respondent at £3OO.

div.head: "Joe Corbett's" Mission.
div.p: "Joe Corbett's" Mission.

The most successful night of the mission to the people by MrJoe Corbett, was undoubtebly Sunday last, when a large concourse of people crowded into the Parr Hall to listea to the spirited and well delivere I address on the parable of " The unfruit- ful tree," by the already well-like I Warrington Evangelist, Joe Corbett. He was accompanied on the platform by Dr Harcourt, Mr Job Swales, Mr Johnson, Mr E Horton, Mr H Wardman and Mr A E Windle. The missioner was extremely original in his remarks, and stated that people were likened to the tree mentioned in the parable and that if a person did not yield good fruit in the way of 1 good living and works, and chose the wicked and wrong path they would undoubtedly be cut off. The missioner urged upon the people the advisabil- ity of choosing the right path, by accepting the Lori Jesus as the Saviour of us all. During the service, Mr Johu Corrin and Mr Pierce A.L.C.M., I sang a duet out of Sankey's "Cut him down" which. ' was a rich musical treat, and later Mr ' Pierce sang a solo with great fervour The Apollo Male Voice Choir sang two selections during the evening, including" Crusaders "which was exceedingly well sung, and special thanks are due to them for the kind assistance they have given to the missioner, and also thanks are due to the Warrington Male Voice Cnoir who so kindly sang on the opening night, and we think that if these two choirs would only unite, Warrington would have one of the finest male choirs in the district. Special thanks were given to the conductor of the Amalgamated Choir, Mr Albert Spruce, and also to the able organist Mr Fred Podmore, M.I.U.M. and the Legh-street Subscription Brass Band gained a hearty vote of thanks for the willingness with , which they so kindly promised to play gratuitously , for this mission. They paraded the streets on 11 Sunday last and played most appropriate music, which was very much appreciated. During the collection, Mr Corbett sang an effective solo. Alto— gether the mission has been very satisfactory. and the attendances have been very gratifying ;so much so that Mr Corbett and his helpers have de- cided to continue same far another month at least.

The deceased. who was at one time fortman at Messrs J Crosfi,ld and Sons', was SO years old, having been employed by them for 55 years, his connection with the works ending April 7tb,1884. div.p: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES

A MOTHERS INHUMAN CONDUCT.—SMIET SENIRCNCE. At the Warrington Police Court on Monday before Mr P Monks and other magistrates, Mary newton, last from the Workhouse. was charged with having been drunk and dis• orderly in Horaemarket-street. on Saturday evening, end alio with having exposed her child, Phoebe Newton. in such a manner as to cause it unnecessary suffering and injury to health.—Mr thowne,proseouted on behalf of the N.5.P.C.0., and said that the prisoner came out of the Workhouse on Saturday morning, bringing the little girl with her. The portress at the Workhouie gave the girl a shawl. At half- past seven on Saturday night P.C.'. Bruin and Cooper saw the prisoner in If orsesnarket-stm-t trying to sing, and etazgering along the road. The child was with her sad Was crying bitterly. The woman was arrested. On the way to the Police Otation she asked where tne child was and on P.C. Bruin telling her that 'it was all right she said "take it away and put it. In the Workhouse." Superintendent Monaghan saw the child at the Police Station and sent for Inspector Hackett. The Child was wet through and very cold. It was taken to the Workhouse The prisoner had previously bad three and six months for neglect of children Some time ago, a home was found for her at Manchester, but she would riot stay there.—She was now sent to gaol for three months.

div.p: MINOR OASES. Warrington Borough Court. BATutthax—Before Messrs T Birchall Oa the chair) and It .

_ Fair°lough. THEFT OF • SAUCEPAN.—Nose Kelly and Bridget O'Brien were charged with stealing from William Thomas. milk- dealer, Fennel-street, between five and seven o'clock on Tuesday night. an iron saucepan, valued 7. 6d They pivoted guilty.—dtmerintendent Monaghan said Mrs Thomas last'saw the satriepan at five o'clock on inesday afternoon, and two hours later she missed It. Information was given to the police, and It was subsequently discovered that the two women had sold the pan to a man ntmed Kowlinson. !hey were arrested, and then admitted having stolen it. Both prisoners had been several times before tha bench previously. and they were Bent to gaol for one month's hard labour. MONDAY.—Before Mr F, Monks (in the chair) and Messrs .
Birohall, Hayward, Vitright and Thornton:.

- AN APPRENTICE LEAVER WORK. —Joseph Lee,B Florenoe-et was charged on a warrant with having left the employment of Francis Joseph Dell, Sankey-street. without permission, putting his employer to a loss of £O.—Defendant said he could not keep himself with the wages he was receiving.— , Mr Dell said he was well treated and received the specified wages.He had been away from work:for 20 months.—An order was made upon the defendant to pay the £lO and costs at the rate of hi per week. WRDNESDAY.—Before Mr Biranall (in the chatr),Alder man Hutchinson, and Mr Geddes. • •

DANGEROUS CHARACTER.—ThOmis Flannery, a labourer, was charged with hiving been drunk and disorderly fu Horeemarket-street on Tuesday evening ; also with assault- ing Samuel Marshall, barman : and further with damaging a copper kettle at the Central Hotel. —P C Clark said be saw the prisoner outside the Central Hotel. He was using bad langusge. Witness went to him and he began to strike out right and left. Witness ebtained the assist- ance of a bystander and toolc prisoner to the Police Station.—aainuel Hartley, barman at the Central Hotel, said the prisoner came into the hotel about eight o'clock, but as he was drunk he refused to serve him. He thereupon picked up a glass which was three parts full of beer. had a drink. and then threw it at witness. He avoided the glass and it struck a copper kettle and dinged it.— Superintendent Monaghan said this was prisoner's 35th appearance. He was a most dangerous character to be at large—in fact. he was one of the worst characters In War- rington.—Prisoner was fined 104 and costs for the first offence. and for the two other offence., was committed to gaol for a month.

DIDN'T KNOW KZ WAS IN CHICSIIRE.—George W Cousins, of Liverpool, was charged with 411114 wfully allowing a certain traction-engine to be used on the highway at Appletoq <re the 25th of January without the same having been register- ed ; and also with a like offence at Stretton on the 4th Yebruary.—He pleaded guilty.—? C Hare said he was on duty at Appleton in company with Superintendent Benton when he saw the e,gine being worked along the road. He asked the dri‘er for his licence. He failed to produce one for that district. but he had one in his possession for the City of Liverpool. lto found that defendant had neither register nor licence for the Coanty of Chester.—Defendant said the driver did not know he was in Cheshire. or he would have obtained • licence. The offences were not intentionally committed. —The Bench imposed a fine of lOs and costs for each offence Tnacriost KNDIND RUNS INTO A HEDGE.—JOSeph Jameson Was summoned for being drunk in oha-ge of a traction engine at Little Legh on January 25th.—lividence was given to the effect that defendant was so drunk that be drove the
-- engine into a beige —d fine of 20s and costs was inflicted, the Chairman remarking that the offence was a serious on as it might have resulted in oonslderable danger to life and limb.
BREVITIES —Michael Rogers was fined 51 for making use of obscene language at Walton, and Albert Houghton was fined 21 for being sleep whilst in charge of a horse and cart at Stocktoa Heath.

div.p: Runcorn Petty Sessions.
MONDAY.—Before Mr Reynolds (in the chair) and Mr W Timmins.

Fuxin's ThaviNG.—Peter Wilson, butcher, Friar-street, was summoned for furiously driving a pony an.i trap on the 7t,n inst.—Prisoner pleaded not guilty.—P Q Wilson deposed that on the date mentioned he saw the defendant come along Church-street at the rate of fifteen miles an hour and he was In immediate danger of colliding with a vehicle. He skidded on the frozen snow and ice and it was a marvel that he did not smash Mr Mlles' window. Witness followed the defend- ant to the house and found the horse smoking like a furnace. —Defendant pleaded that the horse had not been out fot over a week and was consequently restlese. 'the horse had broken the bit. He was not drivingfariously.—Defendant was fined 1 s incluling costs. CONTRAVENTION OF THE RDUCATION ACT.—For neglecting to send their children to school, James Hunt. James Johnson, Mary Morrison. Walter Rose and Amy Dillon ware fined Sc or in default seven days; David Walker and Luke Speed, ;'s 6d or seven days. Pooh RA CASES.—About 54 persons were summoned for non-payment of their poor rate. In the majority of the oases the usual order was made the remainder being settled out of Court.

The postponed match between Warrington and If ndders fie Id was played at Yartown on Wednesday in good weather. Warrington were without Isherwood, the vacancy being filled by Jone, who wai formerly a Hudderifield player. Mr Bruckshaw of Stockport was the referee and the teams lined out as follows _

_ Huddersfield—J Beadybough. bank; L t Deere, W Daw- hint, A Larard, and W F Kitotwn three-quarter backs ; P Dewhirst an Marsden, half backs ; J Conley, P Driver, I Dawson. I Knight, T Dickeneon, F Littlewood, H Naylor and M Sutcliffe. forwards. . _

Warrfugt-on—Hallam, back; Fish. tones, Dickenson and Harris, three-quarter backs ; Edmonds and Hookenhall, half backs; Boardman Morrison. Taylor, Ashton, Swift, Fell, Bdracindson and Roberts,e forward.. Huddersfield won the toss and Warrington kicked off against the wlad. Flay settled for a time in the centre' until Dickenson broke away, sad was only just pulled down by Kitchen near the home line. Readynough brought relief by a good kick, and Deere all but got over the line, just stepping into touch near the visitors' line. The same player directly afterwards was again prominent with anotber flee run, after good passing by Marsden and Walter Dewlatrat. The visiting forwards worked the ball down the field, and Jones made his mark in front of the Huddersfield goal. Fish took the kick, but made a poor attempt at goal. At half time neither side had 'coral.

Sutcliffe kicked off, and Dickenson returned well to the home " 25." Resdyhough replied well to a kick by Harris, which was taken up by 'Meissen and Sutcliffe, bat was spoilt by passing forward. Warrington attacked persistently. powerful punting by Hallan:Land Roberts keeping ths home team in their own ball. There was no score until ten minutes from time when Fish scored for Warrington after fine passing in the home "25." The same player failed at goal. Jones made a good run for Warrington, but was pulled down by Readyliough. Deere mulled, and Fish picked up and scored his second try. Hallam took 'Re kiek, but failed to add the extra points. Result s—Warrlng- ton 2 tries (6 points), Huddersfield nil. SwINTO7f V. BRADFORD.

This match, which had been twice postponed on aecount of frost. was played on Wednesday on the cwinton ground. Owing to the positions the clubs orseupy in the League table this meeting aroused much interest, and in or for to secure a good atteniance of spectators the kick off did not take placs until four o'clock. Both clubs were strongly repre vented the only alteration on the Swint= side being the substitution of Taylor for E Valentine, In the three quarter line Bradford won the toss and Preston commenced the game for Swinton. The visitors quickly attacked, and after a p toeing movement Hager. scored an unimproved try. This was all the scoring up to half time, when Bradford led by three points. Early in the second half Swinton were awarded a penalty kiok and Preston placed a goal. With oaly one point between the teams Bradford played up strongly and Smales scored a try which Mosby easily improves, Then Davies and Morgan set the home beaks going and Taylor scored a try which Preston tailed to improve. A well- contested game ended in a win for Bradford by one goal and two tries (eight points) to 'Minton one goal and one try (live points).
