div.head: NORTHERN UNION. SOUTH WEST LANCASHIRE LEAGUE.
div.p: THE NORTHERN UNION. SOUTH WEST LANCASHIRE LEAGUE.
A Poor Game at Warrington.

The return meals b-tween Warrington and Widnes in the above competition took place on Saturday at, Wilderspool before s,tO'J spectators. Considerable interest was taken Into the encounter owing to the fact Must the championship or the competition lies between these two clubs. Warrington were without Fish and 3 Swift, the vacancies being tilled by Jones and G Jolley. Widnes were at full strength. The ground was in good order, and the teams, under the charge I of Mr Squires of Erotighton, lined out in the following order. I Warrington: Henan:Li:lli back ; Jones, lsherwood.Diosen- son. and Harris, threequarters ; Edmonds and Allen, half books; Boardman, Morrison. Edmondson, Fell, Taylor, Jodey Askton, and J Jolley forwards. Widnes fillay.b mit Peicosk. itispan, Taylor and Hughes three-quarters, 4,uglas and Lady,half-backs; Aspey, Kamp- son. Curtis, Moss, Riley, Rigby, Macdonald, and Hughes forwards.

Aspey kicked off against the wind for Widnes. Taylor returned to Eispan who raulied and the resulting scrimmage gave Jones a chance, but he was smartly tacklel by Douglas. Some exciting work followed in close proximity to the Widnes line, and Tilley had all his work cut out to keep his charge intact. Aspey played very coolly, and by mark. lag saved Widues from disaster on several occasions. Edmonds whose diminutive size rather surprised the spec- tatore, put In some very smart work, and, following up a dribble, he settled Tilley on the line. Good forward work got Widnes out of their tight plots Warrington had all the game, and Widnes only at rare intervals reached the half way line The play was very uninteresting, though the ground was in fair condition, and each side preferred to indulge in too much kicking, open play baieg at a discount. Anne piece of judgment be Edmondss who threw Maws: half way across the field to Jones, was dsservedly applauded and Jones almost got through. lie was, however, tac sled by Hughes and Taylor at the corner fiag. The first really good bit of passing was betweea Edmonds, Dickenson, and Ishervrood, the latter having hard lines in not scoring, Hall-time : Warrington nil, Widnes nil. Taylor restarted and the first few miuutee' play was in midfield. A free kick W. 9 placed for Tille7 beyond half-way, and needless to say. his kick for goal went nowhere ”ear the mark. In faet, it allowed Harris and Dickenson a chance to indulge In a passing run which gained more than half the length of the field This was followed bye dribble by Ed- monds and a follow-up by Harris. who taekled I iltey on his line. A minute later Jones crossed the line, but no try was allowed, though the point was quite a legitimate one However, a free kick again put Warrington close to the Widnes line. The attack only ended in a minor. Widnes although they had the wind, seemed to have fallen off, and rarely reached the half-way line. A fine run through the thick of the team by Hallam, followed up by passing by Jolley and Taylor. caused Widnes much anxiety. and this was followed by passing between Allen, ledmonds and Her-is who was held on the line. Hallam had a kick at goal, which went wide. Widnes were playing for a draw, and they sue. eeeded in their objeot, the match ending with no score.

LEIGH v ST HELENS. This return notch at Leigh proluced a highly interesting game, but there were not more than 1.100 spectators. 2either side was fully represented, Leigh having three and , St. Helene four men away. Lei,do atar3ed, and for a short time St. Helene had the butt of the play, their long kicks keeping Leigh on the deensive. Eventually the Leigh for- wards rushed the ball to the centre, where Towers, seeing a good opening, passed to Causer who, though hotly p4ratied for about thirty yards, kept his lead and scored a grand try. no goal resulting. Play was then even until the interval, when Leigh led by a try to nothing. On resuming, St. Helens kicked off against the wind, and after splendrd oorn- biaation by Bennett and Causer, the former got a flue open- ing, but was called back for a throw forward, Leigh pressed hotly and Johnson dropped a goal. A few moments later Bennett charged down a kick by the full back, and after debb'ing over half the length of the field scored a grand try. Davies failing at goal. After a series of splendid rushes by the home forwards J Roberts scored a try, Towers placing a goal. In the last few minutes St. Helens attacked, and clever play by Doherty ended In Lambert seoring a* Unim- proved try. Result —Leigh. two Oats and three tries (13 points; St. Helens. one try (three points).

div.head: NORTHERN LEAGUE.
div.p: NORTHERN LEAGUE.
SWINTON V. SALFORD,

The return match between these local clubs drew a large crowd of spectators to the Swintoa ground The first match at Salford earlier in the season'ended in a win for that club by two points after a poor game, but Swintoa in this match not only reverseit matters, but won by a very substantial margin. This was entirely due to the marked superiorly of the Swinton backs, whose three-quarters were kept con- tinually busy by Davies and Morgan. and they made the most of the opportunities given to them; From the kick off Salford attacked strongly, arid the game had only been in progress a short time when Lomas dropped a goal. These teams met before a very poor gate on the Lower- house-lane ground. Widnes. on Saturday. The ground was sodden and slushy, so that the players found oonsiderible CM-rutty in running and In keeping their feet. A start was made a few minutes late, the home team failing to turn out punctually. Widnes consequently started against the wind, with three men short, but the absentees all aopeired within the first few minutes of play. At the outset a '• serum " had been formed on the midfield line, and from this the visitors rushed smartly to the Widnes line, when the home- sters were penalized. Nothing came of the kick this being I largely due to the state of the ground and the ball. Alforde attempted to change the venue, but he was pushed into touch. One of the Warrington halves made an excellent breakaway and nearly got over. Warrington continued to have slightly the best of matters. By means of some imert kicking work Widnes got into their opponents quarters where McCabe marked in a favourable position. For some 15 minutes the visitors did well, but at half-time the sheet was still un- marked. Restarting, Warrington rushed down in capital style again, but they were driven back by a huge punt by Alforde. After this the horneaters' form improred irn- mensely,and they seemed until the end to have the better of the game. Bown tried hard to score and was brought down in possession of the ball under the posts. Alforde made an attempt to Erik a goal, but once more the leather fell short. A few minutes from time Widnes were again smartly on the aggressive and after a considerable amount of work on the Warrington line. flown got the chance of a good place kick, and the oval sailed between the uprights in fine style. _ At the eighth meeting of this winter's series, held in the Museum Lecture Room, Mr A Jackson read a paper, one of a series of notes on our local birds, on the robin With the patient and loving care of the true naturalist, Mr Jackson ham watched the redbreast and laid before the club the results of his observations. His notes upon their habits were of exceptional interest ; whilst in addition to much detailed information about their nests and eggs,he pointed out that their habits varied to some extent with locality,and that in respect of many regions they were immigrants. He also alluded to the folk lore of the robin, whose bright red breast and genial audacity seemed to have impressed the popular imagination from the arliest times.

div.head: EMPLOYMENT OF WORKHOUSE INMATES.
div.p: THE EMPLOYMENT OF WORK- HOUSE INMATES.
Sale of Work at the Town Hall.

There was a large gathering of ladies in the Council Chamber at the Town Hall, Warrington, on Tuesday afternoon on the occasion of the annual sale of work in connection with the Warrington Branch of the Brabszm Employment Society, which as our readers are aware, provides pleasant and (slay emr:qoyment for the aged and infirm inmates of the Warrington Workhouse. The sale of work is the chief means by which the society dis- poses of the articles made by the inmates. There was an excellent collection of goods on sale and these were readily bought by the ladies present. A to room had also here provided.

The opening ceremony was performed by the Mayoress (Mrs J C Parr). Mr A J Jolley presided. At the outset, a report on the work of the society was presented by Mrs Eielsten,the secretary. After acknow- ledging the receipt of donations from Mrs Lyon and Mrs Gaddum, who were usable to be present Mrs Edelstein, said poverty and suffering there alwayslwae amongst us, and so far as we could tell it must always be so in this wcrl I. rreir efforts in connection with the Brablzon scheme were a small attempt to alleviate the lot of the aged and infirm in our workhouse—and as there was such deep monotony and sameness in their lives so there was sameness in the circumstances and reports that she haelbrought before them each year.Tney just managed to pay their way, that was to say they had kept their expenditure within tbeir receipts and had a trifling balance in hand of 73 Si They had been steadily and carefully repaying the original loan of £lO to the Central Farad. They now owed £3 104—having paid 303 this year. The remain- der of the profits had been spent on a tea to the inmates of the:Workhouse Infirmary. These numbered about 140—and the item under this head was £4 83. This one tea—just once a rear—was all that they were able to do for their workers except what came from the private generosity of the vatic-rue ladies ; and there appeared to be a feeling in the minds of some of the pupils that the Brabaz en ladies benefltted in some way from their work, perhaps even yocketing the proceeds of the Ulf% (Laughter.) nig was very unfor- tunate, and she wished it was possib'e to do more, but, as she had shown, they only just paid their way. They had ventured on that account to price the articles for sale a !RI le higher this time an as to make more proer, and stm felt sure no one would grudge paying a little more in such a good cause even if they might privately think the things were 'not quite 1 worth the money. (Hear, hear.) They had been much encouraged this year by the advent of four new mem- bers—Mrs John Davies,Mra Edward Wrjght,Miss Nannie Fairclough, and Miss Ethel Roberts. She hoped they would be able, with their assistance to create fresh interest in the work and introduce more varied occupa- tions. This would be the last time that she had the opportunity of appealing to them for support in her present capacity, as she was ceasing to be secretary She proceeded to refer to the appointment of Miss Broadbent as the hon secretary and hoped that the a•cif be might always have extended to it by the Guar- lens and officials the kind encouragement and sympathy which she ventured th think was its due.

The CHAIRMAN said- be bad always been in warm sympathy with the work of the Brabazon E-nployment Society. If he had had big way it would have started sooner than it did. (Bear, bear.) There was,however, some hesitation on the part of his colleagues in allowing the organization to commence work, and nat artogether unjustifiable hesitation. There was a feeling that it might interfere with the work of the institution, as a whole. In some parts of the country societies of this kind had ocoasionally conflicted with the discipline of work- houses. Flo only said this in justification of those who at the first did not see their way to Consent to the scheme being initiated. He ventured to say, how- ever, that those who objected then had since been con- vinced by the logic of facts that they were mistaken. In the hands of ladies who had carded out the work under the supervision of Mrs Edelston, there had never ham any ground for diesatisfaction on the part of the Guardians. Ile felt very deeply indebted to Mrs Edelston for the work she had done during the last five or six years. The Guardians suffered a great loss when she ceased to be a member, and this society was now suffer- ing a grist loss in the severance of her connection with it. Ile was sure, however, that the ladies who worked so diligently and loyally in connection with the society would accord to the new secretary, Miss Broadbent, the name loyal support they had given to Mrs Edelaten. (Applause). The klaYoncs; said that after listening to such an interesting and complete report it was not necessary for her to say anything to commend to them tho merits of the Brabazon Society. She would only express the hope that the goods which had been so nicely made would be quickly bought, so that those who had done the work might have the satisfaction of feeling that their efforts bad been appreciated. (Applause.) She had great pleasure in declaring the sale open. (Applause.) The services of the Mayoress were acknowledged, on the proposition of Miss BESSIE BUTTON, seconded by Mrs CLAY.

div.p: DEAFNESS AND NOSE AND THROAT DISEASES AS A SPECIALITY

As a specialised treatment for Deafness and diseases of the ear, nose, and throat, the methods of the Drouet Institute are meeting with remark- able success. The last issue of the " Supplement to the Journal for the Deaf "contains the detailed reports of twenty-sia cases cured during January by prescriptions issued by the Institute, and dwells upon the f act that nearly one-half, of these patients had tried the usual treatment recommended by ocher specia- lists without deriving benefit. Among the obstinate cases described is that of Mr T E Luke.who was deaf for twenty years, and who bad also suffered at the same time from a chronic nose and throat trouble. Although Mr Luke had doctored in the ordinary way for ye,.: rs without gaining relief, he was net long under the Drouet treatment before obtaining a complete cure, which be describes as fellows :

18, Forest Avenue, Forcist-road, Fishponds, Bristol. February Bed, 1902. Dear Sir,—When I think that a month ago I could not hear my watch tick six inches from my ear, and now I hear it 35 inches I am astonished and wish 1 could per- suade all deaf people to try the Drouet treatment. Dear Sir, will you please print this statement, together with any other facts concerning my case that you think fit to add, in your journal,in the hope that some poor sufferer may see it and be encouraged Co try your treatment, and I feel sure they will be, as I am, only too thankful to recommtrid it to others.—l am, yours thankfully. div.head: DEATH OF MR ROBERT DAVIES. An Honoured Warringtonian's Career.
div.p: DEATH OF MR ROBERT DAVIES. An Honoured Warringtonian's Career.

Warrington has lost another of its most honoured sons by the death of Mr Robert Davies who passed away at his residence, Birch Dale, Stockton Heath, at 7.15 on Xi onday evening. A Warringtonian by birth,Mr Davies was widely esteemed for his many excellent qualities and the news of his death occasioned profound regret. The deceased gentle- man, who was in hi a seventy-sixth year, was the senior solicitor of Warrington' being head of the well-known firm of Robert Davies, Kirkconnel, Davies and Burgess. He had been in failing health I for some little time, suffering from heart weakness and consequent troubles, but his constitution and I the wonderful vitality which he displayed almost to the end bad hitherto enabled him to overcome the attacks which his ailment made upon him. So late as ten days ago Mr Davies visited his office and there was then nothing to indicate that the end was so near. It is believed, however, that during the last few days he contracted a cold or chill, I which developed into bronchitis of an acute form, and it was to this that his death was due Mr Davies consulted several eminent specialists from time to time, and his local medical adviser for many years and up to his recent relinquishment of practice was Mr Charles White. Latterly, and up to the end, Dr Parker had been in attendance, and had been un- remitting in his attention and Care. Genuine and widespread were the expressionF.or regret when the melancholy news of Mr Davies's death became known. By his demise another link with the past has been severed and he will be greatly missed by every one with whom he came into contact. Mr Robert Davies was born at Warrington on the 10th October, 1826, and was the eldest son of the late Mr James Davies, of Warrington, sail canvas manufacturer who during his life was one of the leading men of the town, and filled almost every public office. He was also one of the heads of the Warrington Conservative Asso- ciation. Having:begun his education at the Warrington Grammar School, and: finished lit at :Rugby School, just as Dr Arnold left it, Mr Davies chose the legal prc- fession for his business career, and was admitted as a solicitor in the year 1849. He subsequently became head of the firm of Robert Davies, Kirkconnel, Davies and Burgess of the Market-place. Mr Davies was joint Clerk to the County Magistrates for Lancashire and Cheshire, and Clerk to the Borough Magistrates, and Law Clerk to the Newton and Widnes Local Boards, until the increasing demands and growth of his private practice necessitated his resignation of those appoint- ments, Ho was a Perpirual Commissioner, and held the public offices of Law Clerk to the Governors of Boteler Grammar School and Law Clerk to the Visiting Justices of Haydock Lunatic Asylum. In addition, he had the Crown appointments of Steward of the Manor of Widnes and Steward of the Honour of Halton, both under the Duchy of Lancaster. Mr Davies possessed strong literary and scientific tastes. especially in the direction of Greek and Latin classics, and of botany ; which notwithstanding the calls of his profession, he found leisure to cultivate. He was largely instrumental in the establishment of the Museum Art Gallery, and presented to it a picture by the celebrated artist, Fortuy, and a marble statue by Mr Warrington Wood. He was for some time a member of the Museum and Library Committee, and was also prominently con- nected with the Warrington Literary and Philosophical Society, of which he had several times been president and vice-president. Ira politics, Mr Davies was a Con- servative. and in religion he was a Churchman, and he had wen for many years a manager and the school correspondent of the Stockton Heath'schools. Mr Davies bad often been approached with a view to allowing himself to be nominated as Mayor of the borough, but had always felt that it would be too great a burden, in addition to the other calls upon his time and atZention We uaderetand that Mr Davies was on one occasion approached with a view to becoming a candidate for ' Parliamentary honours but declined to do so. I Be bad been once married—to Miss Agnes Gaskell, daughter of Mr Edward Gaskell, of Birchdale,who predeceased him about two years age—by whom he had four sons, three of whom are now living. As a Warringtonian who took a pride in the town of his birth, Mr Davies was never happier than when recount- ing his rich fund of reminiscences of earlier rime, in "the good old town." He possessed a singularly retentive memory, and could vividly recall the events of seventy years ago. He recollected the burning of Mersey Mills In December, 1830, when he was "taken out of the nurse's arms to see the sky glowing fiery red with the reflection of the flames:" At the Coronation of William IV. he remembered that his mother "made • royal crown, with a crimson velvet and gilt framework, weaving endless ropes and wreaths of laurel, which were ornamented with yellow gourds, and the crown aforesaid, thereby making a royal show in front of the house." Other facts of moment which stood out in his recnlleetion were the alarming visitation of obelus in 1833 ; the time when the windows were bricked up, owing to the window tax; the coaches "rattling through the streets over the cobbles at a hard gallop " ; the old Bridge, " a structure of wood with open railings " the " clear stream in which fishermen were netting sparlings in the season" ; the time when a royal sturgeon, or a salmon might be seen leaping on its way to the weie pool at the island, and he told how at the last-named place he himself " saw 11 salmon spread out on the bank which bad been netted in one afternoon ! "

Mr Davies was of a singularly kinlly and unostentatious disposition, and waa ever ready to lend assistance to any deserving cause. He was a staunch friend of the poor and needy and took a keen interest in every inatitution which had for its object the amelioration of suffering, the spread of education, the happiness of his fellow-tovensm.m, and the m-,rAl and spiritual progress of the people. The church and schools at Stockton Heath received much valuable aid from hint and partisularly in the village will his loss be severely felt, _

As a mark of respect to the dcvased gentlnman the flags at th. Town flail and Coonervative Club were hoisted to half mast immediately on the intimation of his death being received. REFERENCE AT THE LIBERAL CLUB. _

Speaking at a smoking concert and distribution of billiard prizes at the Liberal Club, on Tuesday evening, Mr A El Cronfield alluded in sympathetic terms to the deceased gentleman. He said he int heard the news of Mr Davies's death as ha arrived at Bank Quay Station that evening from London. Mr Davies ITSS an old friend of his (Mr Crosfield's) father and an honqured townsman. His death was another link severed with the past. (Hear, hear.)

div.head: MASTER MARINER'S AC TION•
div.p: A MASTER MARINER'S AC TION•

At the Nisi Prius (bourt, Liverpool, on Wednesday (Before Mr Justice Wills and a common jury) Arthur Anderson,. master of the schooner Emily, trading between Runcorn and Falmouth sought to recover from Thomas Rayner, the amount of surgical expenses in- curred by him in consequence of injuries he sustained whilst ia the service of the ship. tie also claimed for loss of wages. Defendant denied that the injuries were received in the course of plaintiff's duties as master, and if so he submitted they were not liable to him in respect of the losses. Mr Taylor, K.C., and Mr Keogh were coarsel for tb Plaintiff, an Mr florridge, and Mr F E Smith represented defendant. His Lordship held that under the section of the mer- chant shipping act upon which the action was based surgical exPenSes were an absclute charge egaiust the ship, rut with regard to wages the operation of the act stopped when plaintiff was landed, and he was not entitled to charge the amount he had paid to a subSti- tute as an absolute obligation against the shipowners, but should have brought it into account as a 7yaga disbursement. —Judgment was given for plaintiff for £2B medical expenses.

Wycliffe P.S.A. Society. There was an average attendance at the meeting of this Siciety on Sunday. Mr W H Wallington presidel. The musical portion of the service was enriched by the singing of a duet " Now are we ambassadors" by Messrs tiassall and Gough, and the perfo:mance of " The Crusaders" by the members of the Warrington Male Voice Choir. The lart named item is the test piece in a choir competition which is to take place at Earlestown to-day and the choir acquitted themselves in a manner which augured well for their success. The address was delivered by Mr Blaine, of Manchester, who based his remarks on text in Deut. 341 chap. 5 and 6 verses, relating to the deatb of Moses. He proceeded to refer to the punishment of sin,as was exemplified in the life of Moses.—The service was also taken part in by Mr D Owen and Mr F Brown.
Workingmen's Mission Cricket Club.

The annual concert in -connection with t.-1173.above club was held In the Thewlis-snreet School on Mon- day. The attendance was not so large as usual; this no doubt was to be accounted for by the wretched climatic conditions and also by the fact that the concert season is now Adrawing to a close, The presentation of the cup and medals for the bast bowling and batting averages was made by the, Chairman Mr W Jones, who congratulated each member upon his success. Miss Bridge sang "The Swallows" and "The Promise of Life " excellently giving the" Children of the City" in response to an encore for the latter. 31rs Harman who possesses a sweet contralto voice rendered very feelingly the songs " Husheen "and "0, dry those tears.' Miss Nelland delighted her hearers with the mandoline solos "Maritana" and "Barcarolle," Mr A Griffiths was heard to advantage in his songs "The sailor's grave "and "Our Jack." "Honour and Arms' and " The desert," were capitally rendered by Mr IS Pownall, who on being recalled for the last item, sang " Theyeoman's wedding song." Gramaphone selections by Mr J. J. Hesketh were much appre- ciated. The humour of the evening was provided by Mr. Milne (St. Helens) and he capitally sustained the element throughout the evening receiving an ntbusiastic encore for each of his contribution, How we nurse the baby" " The serial story" and .ttre nice girls."

div.head: WAR.
div.p: THE WAR.

Mr. A. H. Crosfield and the War. Mr A H Crosfield opened an adjourned debate on the War in South Africa at the weekly meeting of the Bank Quay Mutual Improvement Society, held in the school- room, Thewlis-street, on Wednesday evening. Mr F Williams presided. His position in regard to this South African War, observed Mr Crosfield, had been a little anomalous because his political sympathies in foreign policy were certainly very largely and very strongly with what was called sane Imperialism. He was not one of the " stand-still" echool at all. In the last generation we had realised more fully than before what empire in the best sense of the word meant to Britishers. (Hear, hear.) In conversation with Bishop Potter, of America, that gentleman told him that in a recent tone of the world, nothing bad so greatly impressed him as the way in wuich one hundred thousand Englishmen controlled three hundred millions of orientals in India and Burmah. We had governed them humanely and in a way which had tended to the advantage , of those Eastern races. It was one of those facts which showed what a powe: for good the British Empire might be in the world and our power as a great nation if properly exercised. (Hear, hear.) He , (Mr Crosfield) had been in Canada and had seen the immense future before Canada. There was also a rapidly developing future before Australia and the best possible lines for us to conduct the empire was not to be contin- ually extending our already enormous boundaries but rather to develop the resources we hadigct andro do our duty to the great populations who had to look to the old country. (Hear, hear.) His sympathies were not with the Little Englander. Be would also like to point out that whatever criticisms he passed on the diplomacy which - preceded the war or the Government's policy concerning it, he had never stood as a critic of , the British Army. On the other hand he thought the army had fought the battle in South Africa with more humanity than any !Aber army in the world would have fought it. (Hear, bear.) He might also add, with as much courage and per- sistency and determination as they would find perhaps in no other army. It veas most unfortunate i that an attempt had been made n some parts of the countryhe was glad to say it was not so in Warring-I ton—to make a certain amount of political capital out , of the suggestion that in criticising the diplomacy of Mr Chamberlain they were criticising what our soldiers had done in the field. What he (Mr Crosfield) had to say on that point was this that if by ill-omened policy we had got into a tight place, the tighter the place the greater the credit of tbe men who bad to tight their way out of it. (Hear, hear.) It gave him great pleasure to endorse very heartily what was said by his brother on the last occasion of the importance of supporting the Volunteer movement. If we wanted to avoid conscription we must look to the greater efficiency of our volunteer forces. (Hear, hear.) Those who were young and could serve as Volunteers were doing their country a grand service by joining the Volunteer corps and those who could in other ways encourage the Volunteer movement ought to do it and in that last remark he certainly coupled the employers of labour who ought as a patriotic duty ta give their men a fair chance of attending the encampments held year after year to improve their training and efficiency. (Hear, bear.) Mr Crosfield then proceeded to refer to the negotiations prior to the war. Be thought they would all agree that what put the fat in the fire was the ill-omened Jameson raid and the unfortunate whitewashing of some of the most conspicuous authors of the raid. He would advise those who were desirous of studying both sides of the question to read Dr Conan Doyle's book on the one hand and Mr Methuen's book on the other. (Hear. hear.) Mr Crcsfield admitted that the Outlanders had grievances but he reminded his hearers that Tory and re-actionary as the Transvaal government was, they ccnsented to concede nine-tenths of what was asked foz. at that time unfortunately the power- ful group who owned Mr Rhodes as their leader -were very anxious for war. They controlled the entire preys of South Africa and the editors and sub- editors whom they appointed were the correspondents of the English press and they sent just the news to England that was wanted to further the policy of Mr Rhodes and his friends. Then Lord Milner instead of maintaining an impartial attitude became a strong par- tisan and sent a cleapatch asking for extreme measures. Reference was made to the speeches of Mr Chamberlain who spoke of ex-President Kruger as a"squeezed sponge" and during the negotiations, Mr Chamberlain raised his terms. After we had cut off the negotiations in the early part of September we kept the Boers waiting for three weeks and in spite of cable aft( r cable we would not tell them what our terms were. In the meantime we hurried out our troops, and were the Boers likely to wait until we had got into the best positions before they struck out to defend themselves ? Referring to the alleged pan- African conspiracy, Mr. Crosfield considered that that was an after-thought brought for- ward to justify the war. We should have been stronger as an empire if we bad founded our Govern- ment in South Africa by consent instead of upon force. Alluding to farm-burning, he said the Government was to blame for sanctioning such a policy and it had gone sadly against the grain for our soldiers to carry out such a policy. When we brought back to South Africa 50,000 Beer prisoners what would be their feelings when they saw that their women and children had died in concentration camps ? The outlook was not too rosy for that reason and for his (Mr Crosfield's) part he be- lieved that even those who weee in authority, if they had their time over again would tell them thatithe game was'scarcely worth the candle. Sir E froward Vincent told them they would have to keep 100,000 men in South Africa after the conclusion of hostilities. Were we strengthening the empire by such a policy ? There was some talk of a fight to a finish. If we succeeded in that, what then ? It was a misguided policy and he was afraid it looked very much like building up in that distant country another and a bitter Ireland. .(Hear, hear and applause.) An interesting discussion followed and at the close Mr Crosfield was thanked for his presence and address.

div.head: MINING NOTES.
div.p: MINING NOTES.
From a Correspondent.

North Sheba shares keep steady, and at the present price of 23 ed are a promising speculation for a sharp rise. The latest reports are to the effect that in the 300 foot level the reef is 15 feet wide, and that it is improv- ing in width as it goes down. It is estimated that under the new regime the mine could be made to pay with an average return of 5 dwt. Samples taken right across the reef are stated to have given an average ratite of over licz. an that the margin is a really ample one. In a buoyant market the shares should see a much higher price. As there is evf ry probability that the next boom will be in Land Shares the public may be well advised to watch the fluctuations in United African ',arida' shares During the past week they have fallen to only 49 which having regard to the statements officially made should render them a ridiculously cheap purchase.

div.head: PEARL INSURANCE COMPANY
div.p: THE PEARL INSURANCE COMPANY
LIMITED.

We again wish to draw our readers attention to the balance sheet of the Pearl Insurance Company Limited published in our advertisement columns. For some time the directors have been working strenuously to obtain a yearly income of one million pounds sterling. Aided by the earnest efforts of the superintendent and canvassers their efforts have at length met with the success they deserve, the total income for the last year amounting to no less a sum than £1,005,988 13s 31. in 1897 the income amounted to £565, 238 123 5d so it will be seen that in four years the company has almost doubled its income. This is without doubt due to the increased enterprise of the company in offering the best possible terms to would be insurers and In adopting that prompt system of paying claims for which the office has become famous. As compared with the previous year there is an increased income of £123,365 153 9d, a fact which speaks volumes for the energy of the officials in increasing their returns during a period of trade depression. , The assets, too, it is satisfactory to note have increased in like proportion. In 1897 the assets stood at £7ld 466 and in 1901 at the handsome sum of £1,429 782. Already a valuation of the Company's business up t ) December last reveals a surplus of £282097 which testifies to the ability of the company to meet all its liabilities should occasion seise. A perusal of the balance sheet will cer- tainly prove interesting and any further information can be obtained from Mr J Alakinson, District Superin- tendent, Victoria-road, Runcorn.

div.p: EAR LESTOWN & NEWTON.
P.S.A.

The usual weekly meeting ot the Earlestown and District P.S.A. Society, was held in the Co-opera- tive Hall on Sunday afternoon. Mr J J Leather- barrow presided, and an address was given by Mr T Ormand. Vocal items were rendered by Miss M Watkins and recitations by Mr J Platt. Miss illiamson presided at the piano.

div.head: _ CRUELTY TO A HORSE AT EARLESTOWN.
div.p: _ CRUELTY TO A HORSE AT EARLESTOWN.

Eiward Lightfoot. of Earlestown, was charged at Newton Patty Sessions, on Thursday, before Messrs T J Gillespie (chairman), W Collingwood, and Colonel Wood, with cruelly ill-treating a horse. Sergeant Clarkson and Police-constable Clarke gave evidence, and said that on the 11th inst the defend- ant was driving a horse and cart laden with green- grocery along some waste land in Market-street, when the wheels of the cart stuck in a hole. Defendant then dealt the horse seven blows with the whipstock. The cart had to be moved with the assistance of five men,--Defendant was fined 20s and costs, and the Chairman said that they were ' only sorry they could not give him a taste of the whip the same that he had given to the poor horse. EARLESTOWN WESLEYAN BAND OF HOPE.

In connection with the above an entertainment was given in the Lecture Hall of the Wesleyan Chapel on Wednesday evening, for the purpose of raising funds towards the Children' Stall at the forthcoming Bazaar. There was a large attendance, principally of children, and the gathering was pre- sided over by Mr G Warburton. In addition to a limelight exhibition of " The Children's letter to God," and miscellaneous views, the following pro- gramme was submitted :—Duet, 'The way to life's success," 0 and S Booth ; recitation. " Little Ellie's recitation," Lily Faragher ; song, "Why do summer roses fade," Eva Jones ; dialogue, " Dolly's Mamma and the Doctor," Nellie Cummings and G Cawley ; laughing song by eight boys; dialogue, " Our pledge," four girls and three boys.
MEMORIAL TABLET TO THE LATE REV CANON WHITLEY.

There has lately been erected in Wargrave Church, a beautiful tablet to the memory of the late Rev Canon Whitley one time Rector of Wargrave and his wife. It is something like 10 years since Canon Whitley died, and a movement has bcen on foot some time,for the purpose of perpetuating his memory, and as a recognition of the services he rendered in connection with the church. Tne de- sign of the stone is unique, and is a credit to the worher, its composition being chiefly of marble and polished granite. Jr. bears the following inscrip- tion in gold :—ln affectionate memory of the Rev John Whitley, M.A., Rector of this parish from 1846 to 1892, Honorary Canon of Liverpool, and Rural Dean of Winwlck, and of Penelope Whitley, his wife. In graceful recognition of their faithful good work this tablet is erected by thbir friends and parishioners."—" Live to live."

div.head: ROWDY IRISHMEN AT RAELESTOWN.
div.p: ROWDY IRISHMEN AT RAELESTOWN.

On Monday night, Market-street, Earlestown,was the scene of an unusual disturbance in which some- thing like 40 Irishmen took part. They had been drinking in a public house, And they became 80 quarrelsome that at 10 minutes before closing time the landlord was compelled to close the house to get rid of them. They went out into the street I and indulged in a faction fight in Market-street, fists and feet being freely use]. Sergeant Ling.; and four constables came on the scene and with much difficulty quelled the disturbance, and eight of the men were conveyed to the Police Station and locked up, the remainder being dispersed. The eight men were brought before Colonel Wood and Sir T J Gillespie at Newton on Tuesday morning charged with being drunk and disorderly and were each fined 103 and costs. A woman who was present in court paid all the fines. The names _of the men were Michael Murray (Haydock), James Hannon (Parr), Timothy Gavan (Sr. Helens), Jahn Healey (flaydock),John Fallon (Haydock),Pstrick Hannon (St • Helens),Martin Creagban(St.Helensl,and Martin Mannion (Haydock).

div.head: LECTURE ON ELECTRICITY IT EARLESTOWN.
div.p: LECTURE ON ELECTRICITY IT EARLESTOWN.

The third lecture of the course promoted by the Newton-in-Makerfield Lectures Committee was given in the Town Hall, Earlestown on Wednesday evening by Professor E W Merchant (Liverpool) on "Thermal and Luminous effects of the Electric current." Mr F J Wood presided and there was a large audience. The L.cturer said he did not think it would be right for him to begin to lecture on the electric current, unless he gave them some account as to how the current was discovered, and what it really was. In the year 1786 a certain physiologist experimented on a certain abstruse physiological suhject,which was to find out the effect of electrical stimula on the nerves of a frog. This was , Galvinia., He began by cutting up a frog's leg, and he dissected the nerves. Whilst working on the frog's leg he found very curious results. When he made a spark on the leg he saw a taitch. The effect of the electrical discharge was to make the frog think it was about to make a spring. It was no- thing new,it was a thing which had been seen time after time before, but he found out that if he took a needle and put it against some other metal and touched that against the frog's leg b got a distinct twitch ; that was the first means of detecting the electric current. Galvinia found out that the same thing which made the frog's leg move when it was stimulated by the electric discharge could be applied by the contact of these two metals, and be was :the first to discover the existence of an electric current. From this point the lecture con- sisted of illustrations by the limelight and practical illustrations from apparatus fixed on the platform, all of which were of the greatest interest, He explained the purpose to which electricity could be applied and pointed out the advanage of heating by this method over those at present in use. He dwelt at some length on the connection between heat and light and explained the methods by which incandescent lamps were produced. He described the heat obtained by the electric furnace and showed how diamonds could be manufactured. Mr C W Emmett moved a vote of thanks to the Lec- turer which was heartily accorded. A similar coin- 1 pliment to the Chairman terminated the meeting.

div.head: NOTES BY THE NAY AT EARLESTOWN.
div.p: NOTES BY THE NAY AT EARLESTOWN.

[BY A CORRESPONDENT] The only incident worthy of notice in this neigh- bourhood this week is the meeting which was held in connection with the candidature of Mr Sam Woods. Originally it was intended to hold an or- ganization meeting, but the magnificent proportion of the gathering doubtless caused the promoters to change their minds at the last moment and they idecided to seize the golden', opportunity of ietro- Aduring the campaign. Consequently Mr Sam Woods had a down-right good innings, and if that meeting is to be taken as a criterion of his candida- ture, I am afraid Colonel Pilkington will receive a severe shaking, if not an actual upset. The meeting was most enthusiastic, and Mr Sam Woods and his supporters could find no cause for complaint in the character of his reception. lie has disclaimed any attachment to any particular political party, and comes out simply as a Labour candidate lie appeals strongly to the colliers and all working- men, and doubtless he will receive a good measure of support from all quarters.
Mr Sam Woods has given Colonel Pilkington fair warning of his intentions, and the lines upon

which he intends to conduct the fight. He admits Colonel Pilkington is a perfect gentleman, but he purposes hitting out strongly in a courteous manner, as from man to man. If the colliers, who certainly control a large voting power are loyal to the Federation, they should vote solid for Sam Woods, and if they do this, there cannot be any doubt what the result will be.
7 he District Coancil elections are approaching but so far the only retiring Councillor known is Dr Patterson, whose expressed reason for retiring, is unique, if not proper.

div.head: EXAMINER. FRIDAY- FEBRUARY 28. 1902
div.p: THE EXAMINER. FRIDAY- FEBRUARY 28. 1902
MR. SAM SAM WOODS AND THE NEWTON DIVISION. Meeting at Earlestown.

A public meeting was held in the Town Hall, Earls- town, on Tuesday evening, to hear an address by Mr Sam Woods, the Labour candidate for the Newton Division in Parliament, and others. There was an en- couraging audience over which Mr David Williams pre- sided, supported by Messrs T Glover, J S Walsh, 8 Harvey, 0 France, &o. The Chairman said he was extremely surprised that he had been called upon to preside over that meeting, but he would not like to see such a meeting as that lost for the want of a chairman. That was the first occasion on which be had stepped on to a political platform, and he had done so now because the miners had taken the step they had done in bringing out a Labour candidate. It might be considered that Mr Woods had changed his mind. He might have been a Liberal, but he was per- fectly justified in altering his mind and coming forward as a Labour candidate. There was nothing wrong about it. Their present member was once a Liberal, then he was a Liberal Unionist, and he was a Conservative now. so that they would not be justified in impeaching Mr Woods, as some of them might be under the impression that he had changed his political opinions. He comtili- mented the Miners' Federation for haviug awakened, and that they intended to adopt the policy of direct Labour representation. (Hear, hear.) He contended ' that Mr Woods was a man of ballast, tact, foresight,and judgment, and one who was deeply interested teeth in the domestic and industrial programme. (Applause). Mr Sam Woods said he did not know that he had any- thing to explain away in his past career, but he was going to explain his position to that magnificent meet- ing. He noticed that their respected member and some of his friends had boon having a meeting a short time ago, and his (the speaker's) appearance on the scene seemed to have disturbed their preconceived ideas. They expected to have another walk over, but he (Mr Woods) did not think this should be allowed. He hoped that with the support and co-operation of the working men in that division, they wouid let them see that they had sailed into the harbour prosperously. He had deter- mined to leave political policy and political doctrine to future meetings and to give a few honest reasons as to his plan of campaign which he intended to pursue dur- ing his candidature. He would speak of Colonel Pilking- too as a perfect gentlemen and not one word would pass his lips otherwise than Le say that he was a gentleman. (Hear, hear).l He did not intend to deal in personalities, because blows of that kind at times recoiled on their own head, and if their opponents would be as fair to them, as they would try te be, when the election came off, it would be a model ;election. (Hear, hear). He would, hewever, criticise as strongly as he could any votes given by Colonel Pilkineton. tie would divide his remarks into three heath. Why am I contesting the Newton Division ? Why am I coming out as a labour candidate, and why am I opposing Colonel Pilkington ? To the first he would say because he was a native of Newton. He called it his own Division ever since the redistribution of seats, and he once bad the honour of attending with their pre- sent member to meet Colonel fecCorquorialo in connec- tion with the Miners Federation. It was one of the points in the miners programme that candidates should fight in the division ia which they lived. He had spent the whole of his life according to hie lights, knowledge and judgment to elevate his fellow workingmen, and he did not think there was a working rasa in the country who could say an unfair -went about him. His next reason why he contested the Newton Division was because it was an industrial division, audit would be a burning shame to the working men of the Newton Divi- sion if they did not carry their flag to win. H 3 boasted to having done some good in the Newton Division, organising the Haydock miners, and very Materially , improving their position. He came out wearing no colours but Labour colours, an I he would give no pledges to any but the Labour party. But he would take all the support which could be given him by any party. He would address Liberal meetings, Conserva- tive meetines, Irish meetings, Socialist me. tinge, Orange meetings, and any meeting where they would give him a hearing. He thought be was justified in coming out as a Labour candidate, because of the present positi on of the Liberal party. It was a thousand pities that there should be the disruption which had appeared in I the Liberal party at the present time, and he thought he was much safer in being a Labour candidate. The Labour party was tne greatest patty of all. They would have a direct issue at the neat election in this Division, they would have a capitalist cm the one side and a direct Labour candidate on the other, and if they were interested in the welfare of the workiogmeo, they would not hesitate as to which candidate to support when the opportanity was given them at the next 'election. Why did he oppose Colonel Pilkington ? The democracy of this country had made great progress during the lest 30 years, at the same time there was much left undone. They wanted to improve the laws under which they lived, they wanted to break those burdens which bound them down,land theylwanted to make the laws of England as fair to the workingmen, as they now operated for the rich. He would try to show them that by the votes which Colonel Pilkington had given in the House of Commons, he was not a fit representative of that division. He gave several instances where Colonel Pilkington had voted against measures which were for the beneet of the workingmen, amongst oteers the Miners Eight Hours dill—and it was his action on this measure which prompted him (Mr Woods)in corning out against their member. He wanted every man in that room to exercise the talent of observation, to look round at the poverty and destitution of the country, which would not be improved until they got direct representation from the classes of the people who by sympathy and practice were in close toueh with the people,and if they rallied round him at the next election they would strike such a blow as would reverberate from one end of the country to the other. (Applause.) The Chairman then moved "That this meeting having heard Mr Sam Woods, the labour candidate for the Newton Parliamentary Division, considered that he was a fit and proper person to represent the Division in Parliament, and pledges itself to support him and en- deavour te secure his return at the next election for the Division." Mr 0 France seconded. Mr T Glover speakine in support of the resolution, said it was to the working men they wanted to appeal, and they wanted to clearly point out to them that it was for their benefit and their benefit alone that they wanted to put men like Mr Woods into the House of Commons for the purpose of bettering their position in this country, Mr Woods had pointed out what their representative had done, even in the Sessions of Parlia- ment before this, thee he had not been in sympathy with the workers of this division and had not voted for the interest of the division, and for the workers of the country. If that was so, it was for the workers of the division to say and make up their minds that it was no use sending such a representative to the House of Com- mons if be was going there for the purpose of represent- ing his own interest and not the interest of the people he represented. (Applause.) Mr S Walsh, Mr G Harvey and Mr H Swift also spoke in support of the resolution, which on being put to the meeting was unanimously carried. Mr Wocds thanked them for their confidence and hoped they would pull together and keep from quarrel- ling. _ _
A vote of thanks to the Chairman terminated the meeting.

Barlestown played their strongest available eleven, while the Soldiers were also fully represented. There was a good attendance preset. An exciting game resulted in a victory for Barlostown by four goals to two.
