div.head: CHRISTIAN ENDEAVOUR MOVEMENT.
div.p: THE CHRISTIAN ENDEAVOUR MOVEMENT.

Annual Convention at Warrington. There was a very encouraging attendance at the annual convention in coinnection with the Warrington and District Union of 'Young People's Societies of Christian Endeavour which was held; in Friars' Green Chapel on Saturday afternoon and evening. The societies comprising the Union were well represented and the meetings were attended with gratifying suc- cess. The proceedings in the afternoon commenced with a devotional meeting which was conducted by Mr A Jolley. Afterwards the President of the Union (Rev J F Matthews) took the chair and delivered a brief address. He said his past three years' work as the Vice-President and President of the Union had entailed the sacrifice of a great deal of time and had nlcessitated a great Ideal of preparation, and whether it had done good Cu the individual members of the societies and the societies themselves or not, it had at least been fraught with blessing to himself. He had felt some little reward also in having watched what seemed to him to have been a revival of enthusiasm and interest on the part of the young men connected with the churches with which their societies were associated, and he ventured to think that the presence of so many young men at the Con- vention was some witnese to the revival which he hoped would be long sustained. His final message to them as President was the advice given by the Apostle Paul,"Like heed to thyself." The Christian Endeavour movement was now no new thing. ID had reached its level among the ctlaer religious movements of the day, and would be , finally judged not merely by its power to win the young and to obtain their loyalty and affection, but to touch the intellect and the conscience and to provoke young men especially to their highest intellectual efforts and to win their mos:, sturdy homage to the Master. But if this was to be done "Take heed to Toy ways " must net merely be the dominant force controlling them, but the supreme ambition of the whole associated societies in the Union. The speaker concluded by giving some sound advice to the members.

Mr A MOUNFIELD addressed the gathering and referre to the future prospects of the movement. He said the Christian Endeavour movement had hit upon the secret of prosperity and success because it was seeking to enlist the children in the cause. The best way to ensure success in the future was to instil into the hearts of the children the ideas which they (adults) cherisned Miss rhomasson, leader of the /Junior Society at Newton-le-Willows Congregational Church, read a thoughtful paper on " junior work." At the outset she said she did not know of any movement which had had so short an existence and achieved so great a magni- tude as the Junior Branch of the Christian Endeavour movement. Its development had been miraculous arid carried the mind back to the unique days of the early Christiarr. It had been truly said that the Spirit of God had been in that movement—a move- ment which she thought had far exceeded the anticipations ot its initiators and had before it a future which 'filled one with glowing expec- tations and hope. It had been instrumental in bringing to light Elie utility of the children in the service of the Master ;it had opened out fields of labour which were being entered upcn effectually by the young ; it had demonstrated the infinite possibilities of usefulness which the young were able to accomplish when their aspirations were directed to the definite spheres of the movement. It was a noble work in that it directed the young to put into practical operation and carry into effect the lofty principles of Christianity. Junior work was certainly the inspiration of the high- est possible ideals in life, and must in the near future manifest its power and influence by the noble citizens and practical Christians it would undoubtedly make. She looked upon the movement as one of the most im- portant branchei of Christian srvicc, aslit was to the juniors that they must look to carry on the warfare against sin. Miss L M Ginsos, of Manchester, gave an address on " Chtistian Endeavour in everything," which was listened to with great interest. The speaker urged her hearers to introduce Christianity into their every day life and at the same time to endeavour to train their intellect by taking par% in the work of the Christian hndeavour S xi ties. Some discussion easued relative to the addresses aad to the Christian Eadeavour work in general and the sing ing of:a hymn concluded the meeting. The members then adjourned to the schoolroom where a capital tea was served.
THE EVENING MEETING. REV E T REED'S PRESIDENTIAL ADDRESS.

Another meeting was held in the evening. After de- votional exercises, the retiring President (Rev J F Matthews) delivered his final speech in that capacity and introduced the new President (Rev E T Reed). The speaker heartily thanked the members who had held the office of secretary during the two years he had pre- sided over the Union for their kindness and cordiality in assisting him in the discharge of his duties, and the whole of the members of the societies for the manner in which they had received his visits. It had afforded him much gratification to be brought into contact with the young people of their societies, and he had sought Co bring himself into touch with every Endeavourer.ft was now his very pleasing duty to ask his dear friend. thellev E 'r Reed, to take his place as President, and be trusted they would give Mr Reed the same cordial support, generous assistance, warm sympathy, and prayers that he believed they had given him. Addressing Mr Reed, the speaker expressed the bop • that at the close of his year of office he might find the Union had grown wonderfully under his guidance. (Applaus .). The Rev E T Reed then took the chair and in the course of.his address said that was not the first time he had had the privilege of holding the office of President of the Union. As he stood before them his mind went back to nearly ten years ago when he had the privilege of commencing the first Christian Endeavour Society in the town, and when he knew that some of the members present at the afternoon meeting dated their conversion from that time, his heart was fitled with thankfulness for what God had done during the tan years he had been able to give information and advice to others in the t3wo and neighbourhood who had wished to commence a similar work. As they were aware,the Union had grown very encouraging ly, although during the past twelve months one portion of it had decided to carry on its work from another centre. On that point, however, they might be really thankful because they believed their friends in Widnes and neighbourhood would carry on their work more efficiently from that centre than if they bad remained with the Warrington Union. For the first three years of the existence of the Union he held the office of President and again during the year which ended in 1899 he had the privilege of occupying that position. He never expected that he would be called upon to act as President again and when his name was brought forward in com- mittee some little time ago he expressed his strong desire not to be elected. When, however, there seemed to be a very earnest wish on the patt of the members that he should consent, he did not feel it would be right in loyalty to Christ to hold beck. Continuing the rev. gentleman expressed hie willingness to help the different societies as far as possible if they felt the need of his assistance. Re thsn proceeded to refer to the principles of the Christian Endeavour movement, which he said could be conveniently divided into three sections. First he spoke "4 those principles which related to the Endea- vourer's individual life—personal devotion to their Divine Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, loyalty to the Eudeavour pledge, faithfulness in committee work, loyalty to the church w th which each society was con- nected, and interdenominational spiritual fellowship. Speaking on the subject of loyalty to the church with which they ta twere identified, he said 7they found that those members were the most earnest believers in the spiritual fellowship which they all rejoiced in in connection withithat movement, who were loyal to the church of their own denomination. He did not think that in • Christian Endeavour Society they ought to emphasise their denominational differences. It seemed to him that as time went on the differences which existed between Christian denominations would be less,aad that one great esseatial spiritual communion would be realized more and more. Proceeding Mr Reed touched upon the principles which affected the Endeavourer's life in the world, and urged upon his hearers to abhor drinking, gambling and impurity. The movement,. he said, • upheld temperance, law, order, Sabbath keeping, and a pure political atmosphere. It was with very great regret that he had seen during the last few weeks the example of some in very bigh quarters in this country with regard t) the keeping of the Sabbath, and he was delighted to see that one Presbyterian minister in London had been faithful enough to speak-out on what he (the speaker) conceived to be the ill-advised example of Royalty in patronizing a concert one Sunday and a picture gallery another Sunday. Continuing, the speaker said the Christian Endeavour movement did not ally itself with any political party, but sought through its individual members to permeate and influence all Parties and communities. He impressed upon his hearers the duty of supporting missionary organizations and said the ultimate aim of Christian Endeavour was to evangelise the world. The great facts with which they were face to face led them to see that God wished them to take wide views of their responsibilities and differences in these days. He thought the object of the raising up of such a movement as that was that the way could be prepared for the wider evangelisation of the millions of people who had never heard the name of Jesus Christ. (App'ause.) Miss VANDA TAYLOR, the secretary, submitted the annual report which stated that at the commence- ment of the year they 'had fifteen Young Peop'e's Societies, but last September their Widnes friends, with the hearty consent of the executive, severed their con- nection with the Warriogton Union and formed the Widnes and District Union. At present there were twelve Young People's Societies, with 264 active mem- bers and 136 associates, making a total of 400 members The Junior societies were in a very flourishing con-

ditiort. There were seven societies affiliated with the Union having a membership of 350. The report also stated that there was a strong missionary spirit exist- ing in the societies, subscriptions having: been sent to toreign missions and special meetings addressed by missionaries having been held. Nor had the work at home been forgotten. The Young People's Societies had subscribed to horns missions and held poor children's treats and the juniors had had vegetable collections for the poor and sent fruit to the inmates of the Workhouse. Endeavourers bad engaged in open air work and it was hoped that in the coming summer the Union would make a greater effor to win the MiSieS for Chtist. The Rev C FINCH delivered an ad lress in which he gave advice to the members with regard to 01.:r spiritual life. _

It Mr W Ii EIOPE, of Liverpool. also spoke, and referred to the importancel of the movement as regarded the training of children. He said the great hope of the movement lay in the Junior SOCieCi6S. The principle of the Societies was that every child present at a meeting must take some part and by this means their interest in the work was stimulated. Mr Hope gave some highly interesting details of his work among the destitute chil- dren of Liverpool and at the conclusion was heartily applauded. The pronouncing of the Benediction brought the meet- ing to a close.

div.head: MR. A. H. CROSFIELD AT THE LIBERAL CLUB.
div.p: MR. A. H. CROSFIELD AT THE LIBERAL CLUB.

There was a pleasant gathering in the Reading Room at the Liberal Club, Warrington, on Tuesday evening, on the occasion of the distribution of prizes to the successful competitors in the Christ- mas billiard handicap. Mr. A. H. Crosfisld. the generous donor of the prizes, made the presenta- tion. The room was filled to overflowing. Amongst those present were :—Councillor Tinnion. Councillor Plimpton, Councillor Wilkinson, Mr J Critchley, Mr Bibby, Mr Locker, Mr E A 6anders, Mr Davies, and Mr Thomas Pemberton(hoo. secretary).The pro- ceedings took the form ;of a smoking concert. and , they passed off in a very successful manner. Coun- cilor Tinnion presided. The programme opened with a well-executed pianoforte solo by Mr W H Kendrick, and this was followed by a solo entitled " The Maid of Malabar,' in which Mr S Hassall's pure toned tenor voice was heard to great advantage. An instrumental trio "The Chough and Crow" by Messrs F Davies (oboe), W Hipkiss (clarionette), and R E Warburton (bassoon) was given with tastb and precision. Mr G Gough gave an efficient rendering of the solo The Young Royalist," and humorous songs were contributed by Mr J Emson and Mr II Price. The whistling solo " The Captive Bird," by Mr W Whittaker, was exceptionally well given.

div.head: DONOR O 1 THE PRIZES.
div.p: THE DONOR O 1 THE PRIZES.

During an interval, the CHAIRMAN Proposed a vote of thanks to the donor of the prizes. In doing so, he referred in feeling terms Co the great ser- vices of the late Mr John Crostield, and expressed his heart-felt sympathy with Mr Arthur Crostield and family in their great trial and bereavement. There were many members of the party who had known Mr John Crosfield longer and better than he (the speaker, had done, but they did not and could not appreciate his true worth more, not only as a citizen but as a man and as a member of the Liberal party. (Hear, hear.) In the death of Mr John Croatiald they had lost not only an honoured but a revered leader, and a kind friend. (Hear, hear.) Referring to Mr Arthur Croafiell's generosity in contributing the prizes for the billiard handicap, he said that was only a small token of his desire to do all he could to further the best interests of the club. He was now the head of one of the most respected, and deservedly respected families in the neighbourhood, and they were proud tu know that he fulfilled in an eminent degree all the character- istics of the late Mr. John Crostield. (Applause.) In Mr Arthur Crosfield, the traditions of the Cros- field family would lose nothing of their worth and lustre ([Lear, hear.) Councillor PLUMPTON seconded the vote of thanks. In the late Mr John Crosfield they bad lost a great friend and an all-round man who had done the best he could for his party and the people, whom he had lived and worked amongst. The whole town re- spected him for it and felt his loss very keenly, (Applause). Alluding to Mr Arthur Crostield he said he had the interests of the Liberal Club at heart, and sometimes it was felt he was doing too much for it, His presence amongst them always acted like magic. (Applause). The resolution was carried with great heartiness.

div.head: PRIZE LIST.
div.p: THE PRIZE LIST.

Mr CROSFIELD then distributed the prizes. The following is a list of the winners and tile prizes awarded :-1, tea service, Mr L Auckland; 2, spirit kettle, Mr E Pierpoint ; 3, cruet, Mr Joseph Rigby; 4, salad bowl, Mr A J Jones; 5, teapot, Sergeant- Major Cleland ; 6, marble clock, Mr S J Beaman ; 7, egg stand, Mr fl Williams ; S. case of carvers, Mr C Jordan; 9, barometer, Mr E V Walker; 10, jam dish and spoon, Mr E Wilson •, 11, biscuit barrel, Mr J Mitc'ell; 12, cruet, Mr D Tinnion ; 13, butter shall, Mr W Bibby ; 14, carvers, Mr W Whittaker ; 15 carvers, Mr J Worrell ; and 16, matchb3x, Mr J McKenzie.

div.head: MR. A A CROSFIELD AND LIBERAL DIFFERENCES. _ A. .
div.p: MR. A A CROSFIELD AND LIBERAL DIFFERENCES. _ A. .

Mr CROSFIELD, who was warmly applauded on rising, to address tne meeting, thanked all present for the kind reference to his late father. Ills death was, he said, a , groat loss to the family and himself, because he had never had so close and so kind a friend as he had had In his father. His ;death was a loss to the club, to Liberalism and the good mid town. (Applause.) Pro- ceeding to speak upon political matters he said the kind and cordial invitation he received from Sir Pemberton to join their friendly circle that night was accompanied by a hint that instead of the little political discussion which was generally sandwiched in between the more attractive parts of the'programme—(laughter)—oe these ' occasions they would prefer to hear something of one'a experiences in America, including what he saw of the great yacht race. He dared say some of them thought that would be a pleasanter topic to occupy them than politics at a moment when Liberals were supposed to be rather down on their luck. Still, before treating them to any traveller's tales, it was only right to say a word or two about the unfortunate personal issue which had arisen in their party, and which, in his humble opinion, was not only in the interest of the country dealorable, but also most unnecessary ; not that he ' would appear to exaggerate what ought to be, and they all hoped would be,but a passing difference of metaphor In some quarters people had made great baste to bid Lord Rosebery farewell, but these parting messages were absurdly and utterly mistaken. He agreed with the " Westminster Gszatte " that people could not stand by with equanimity and see his great influence lost to the Liberal cause. (Applause.) What was the usa of hair. splitting and quarrelling about phrases? The " clean slate" might not be a very happy expression, but they could all see now teat the Newcastle programme as a matter of political tactics was overloaded. They would remember John Bright's famous metaphor about the folly of trying to drive half a dozen 'buses abreast through Temple Bar ; so if Lord Rosebery's expression merely meant the revision of Liberal methods, and a concentration of energy upon definite aims, who wou'd quarrel with that ? They were all at one vs ith him. If* politics, as in business, while fighting for their principles they must grasp their opportunities. Then to take the question of Home Rule which had most to do scitn Chia aifEculty, just let him quote what Sir Henry Campbell Bannerman had beers saying :—" I am not prepared to erase from the tablets of my creed any princrple, or measure, or propesal or idra!, or aspiration of Liberalism. That is why I adhere to this o!d policy. as to the general purpose of which, at least, it is not likely that it would take the shape of former BiliE, but it may fall in with a wider scheme of devolution. It is not within the range of pr sctical politics, because at the present moment it does . not commend itself to the English people " Nlav be (Mr Cro-field) heard Lord Rosebery in the Philharmonic the other might speak of building a superstructure in the future on the Irish County Councils. He bad also, like Sir Henry, spoken of devolutim,and the latter saw,they all saw, that Home Rule was not at the present moment a matter of practical petit:ice. It would pass the wit of a Philadelphia lawyer to define such microscopic differ— ences, and surely it was too sad that there should be friction and estrangement upon some hypothetical !question of the future. Devolution would come in the future, whether it was called by " Home Rule " or be I some other name, and all the better if it formed part of the scheme of Imperial Federation which would necessi- tate unloading some of the burden the present Parliament at Westminster carried. But why in the name of common sense were they to anticipate hypo- thetical differences at that future time ? There was not a Liberal in the party who would listen to an indepen- dent Parliament for Ireland any morn than he would listen to separatinn. There was only one other matter on which he would detain them, and which was referred to in Lord Roseberv's letter, and that was, of course, the war. As rrgarded what preceded the war and the diplomacy which led up to it, some of them had most frankly differed from Lord Rosebery about that past history. But as to our present policy in this wet', the eloquent and powerful speech which he deliverol at Chesterfield and to which he (Mr Crnsfield) listened,was accepted by practically the whole of the Liberal party, and if they took the other speeches, such as the power• ml speech to the Junior Reform Club in Liverpool the other day, which he also heard, he believed Sir Henry Campbell-Bannerman would endorse every word of it. Why then were points of agreement on major islands to be ignored, and minor points of difference to be accentuated ? Admit if they would that Lord Rose- bery was a less advanced Liberal than some members of the party ; admit difference of opinion ; had it not hap- ,

pened before? Even he could remember what a thorn in the flesh "Joe" Chamberlain, with his Radical ideas, was to men of the more Whiggish type, such as the then Lord Hartington, and they all knew that Bright and Cobden worked for the Liberal Party, with Palmerston as Premier, though the differences between them were far and away beyond an7thing that could or did exist between the views of Sir Henry and Lord Rosebery. There were peacemakers at work ; let them, then, wish them well. And for the rest, they must bear these troublesome events with patieece and fortitude. Let their leaders settle their personal affairs and let them remember that the great reforms which year by year grew more urgent and more pressing, particularly for the benefit of great working class constituencies like Warrington, education, temperance on the lines of Lord Peers report, and the all. important allied questions, the taxation of ground rents and the housing of the working classes ; that reforms such as these of the first magnitude would neve be dealt with in the best interests ot the community at large until they were carried by the efforts of the Liberal party. Over 90 per cent, of the members of that club belonged to the working class. They all had a direct and vital interest in these measures, and it was to them as time went on they must look for the backing that was to help them to carry them through. (Applause.) Yes, and loyal as they are and would continue to be to their couregeous leader in the House of Commons, and deeply grateful to him, they would hope, notwithstand- ing temporary differences, that when the time came for carrying these reforms, they would also have the assist- ance of Lard Rosebery's powerful, gifted and brilliant personality, and, above all, the assistance of his incom- parable services in the direction of England's foreign policy, in respect of which he was head aod , shoulders above any living man. His friend. Mr Edward Evans summed up the situation for them I when he simply put it last night in Liver- ' pool that they needed both leaders. (Applause.) Mr Crosfield then gave some interesting reminiscences, of the great American yacht race, and, in conclusion said that Sir Thomas Lipton had done a good evor. Be took his boating cheerfully and raised himself to a very high position in the estimation of the Americans. He had helped to create a better feeling between the Americans and ourselves. (Applause). The remainder of the musical pregramme was then given. Another instrumental trio was given by Messrs Davies, Hipkiss and Warburton, and Mr Hipkins also contributed a elle. Songs were also given by Mr Hassall,Mr Gough, Mr J D Brimmelo sr. There were further humorous songs by Mr Ernson, and Mr E A Sanders delighted the audience by his recitation. The duties of accompanist were diseharged by Mr Kendrick.

div.head: WARRINGTON BOARD OF
div.p: WARRINGTON BOARD OF
GUARDIANS,

This Board met in the Board Room at the Workhouse on Wednesday morning. Mr A J Jolley presided and there were present Dr Patterson (vice-ohairman), Mrs Clay, Dr Murray, Rev Faber Wilson, Messrs S Davies. J Clarke, J Payton, W Robinson, J Billinge, T H Ashcroft, A Jolley, J Ball, G Pilling. W Houghton, R Forshaw, G Maher, J Backhouse, A Brooks, with J C Sutton (clerk), and A Wright (Superintendent Padgate Schools.) :INCREASE IN THE COUNTY RATE. Yrlo CLERIC announced that compared with last year the county rate call is £233 4s lid more, but it only exceeds the Clerk's estimate of what it would be by £2223 Si.

Mr PILLING said he was sorry to find that the county rate was advancing. In the Cheshire Unions it was considerably less. lie supposed the time would come when they in the Warrington Union would be in the same pnsitiou.

. -- RESIGNATION OF THE ASSISTANT MATRON. At a meeting of the [loose Committee, Messrs Brooks, A J Jolley, Hickman, and Mather were appointed to confer with Messrs Owen. architects, upon the state of the battery, the condition ther2ol being unsafe, and with authority to act as may be advisable.—me resig- nation of Nurse Taylor, and also ef Clara Addison, a hospital servant, were accepted, and it was decided that the Clerk prepare a testimonial favourable to Nurse Taylor in respect of her three years' service. Nurse F Perry was appointed at a salary of £25 with uniform, rations, &c., and Mr H M Sutton, of Croydon, as temporary clerk to the master, terms £2 23 per week with hoard and rations, the appointment to 13e suLject to one week's notice.—At a meeting held on the 21st February, it was recommended that the resignation of Miss Ward, assistant matron, be accepted, and that a testimonial be granted ; tqat instead of an assistant matron to succeed Miss Ward, a master's clerk be advertised for at a salary of £llO per annum, with rations and apartments ; that the cottage of master and matron be made on March 25th. Mr BROOK 3 moved, and Mr AsucaoFr seconded the passing of the minutes.

Mr l'intatioE asked for further information respecting the appointment of a master's clerk. The CitainueN explained that it was proposed to ap- point a resident master's clerk to aasist the new master and matron, instead of appointing ao assistant matron. It was inevitable that there would be a number of changes. The minutes were then agreed to. LErrER FROM rHE MATROS,—THE BOARD THANKED.

The following letter vr&d read from Mrs Ward :—'• AS this will be the last meeting I shall be able to address you in my official capacity as matron of your Work- house and infirmary, may I claim a little time to C3O- - the conditions under whion I am leaving your service? It is with much pain and regret that I write you, for to me it ;will be parting net only from em- -plovers, but friends. Owing to pressure of work and mental strain and anxieties I have had,of late years,my healta has not always been equal to the demands made upon me. Still, during the wnole of my fifteen years' work I can truly say that the first and sole aim has been to serve you well, and, although the work and respon- sibilities have increased with the necessary changes you have brought about in making better provision for the sick, aged and insan la mates, together with the oars of an increased staff, my interests in work and people have not changed, Why I give up my work you all know, and, whilst thanking the Board on behalf of Mr Ward and myself for all past consideration,l feel certain I can safely leave in your hands the further considera- tion of your kind resolution of December 4th, respect- ing the length of service you wile determine on." The CHAIRMLN said the further consideration of the resolution referred to in Mrs Ward's letter would take place next month. CENTRAL POOR LAW CONFERENCE. It was oecided that the Chairman, senior Vice-Chair- man and the Clerk be appointed a deputation to attend the Central Poor Law Conference (30th annual) to be held at the Guild Hall, London, under the presidency of the Right Ron Viscount Cross, G.C.8., on Tuesday and Wednesday, March 11th and 12th.

div.head: TREATMENT OF SINE EPILEPTICS.
div.p: THE TREATMENT OF SINE EPILEPTICS.

The Chairman was appointed to represent the Board at a conference, soon to he he'd, of representatives of Lancashire Boards of Guardians re sane epileptics, a communication having been received from the Black- burn Board of Guardians to the effect " that it is desirable provision should be made for the separate treatment and care of sane epileptics, and that a Repre- sentative Committee b 3 appointed to inquire into the whole inattsr,and to draw up a report." This was all the business of public interest.

div.head: PEN KETH.
div.p: PEN KETH.

CONCE2T.—A large and appreciative audience assembled at the Wesleyan Schoolroom en Friday last at the concert promoted by the Fenketh Tannery Brads Band. The Band Committee, as usual, had provided an excellent programme and their efforts met with the success they deserved. The object of the concert was to raise funds to enable the members to obtain further tuition, and from their excellent progress so far, they should soon he in the front rank of local bands. The two selections" Vesper Hymn " and ",Rousseau's dream " were very tastefully rendered,as also were the trombone trio " Three jolly sailors," and the quartette " Murmur- ing breezes," Mr William Kilduff was to the fore with the old favourite " Alice where art thou " and the two dramatic selections " Christmas day in the Workhouse," and" The Uncle." The Apollo Male Voice , Choir, under the leadership of Mr T Brough was very I well received, and deservedly recalled lb* a masterly rendering of " Here's life and health," and" On the March." Miss L Davies bf Elollinfare sang the two songs " Leonine," and " A merry heart," in a way that met with the approbation of the audience. Mr E H Pearce sang " The distant shore," and also gave a vigorous ren- dering of the song" Revenge." The humour was sup- plied by Mr Matt Kilduff, whose talent in this respect is too well known to need eulogy. His most successful items wer, " A country concert," and " All of a ditherum," and needless ha say he was recalled for each contribution. The Band was under the leadership of Mr J Harper of Widnes, and Mr B Wilkes, A.L.C.m. ac- eompanied the artistes on the pianoforte.

MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT ASSOCIATION.--This session has certainly been one of the most ;successful kr some time and the meeting of Wednesday night last, one of the most intereFtini,. The subject was "The sea, and the ships on it," and it was in the able hands of Mr Henry Is Wortley, naval architect. The lecturer, handled his subject in a style that showed his familiarity with the subject, and brought his hearers fr3m the day of the earliest vessels known to the present latest man-o'-war and liner. A large and intereeing number of views was thrown on the screen by Mr J IYodward, and the large enjoyed audience thoroughly the evening. A vote of thanks proposed b Mr C E Parker (chairman) and seconded by Dr Murray closed the meeting. THE LATE MR. W. J. BRYTT.--Another well known and respected resident of Penketh, in the persin of Mr W Brett, Passed away on Monday last. Mr Brett has for some time been suffering fr3in a painful illness, and succumbed as stated, at his residence, Greystone Lodge. His death is generally deplored, and the interment at the Friends' Burial ground on Wednesday was attended by a large number of relatives and friends.

div.head: MUNICIPAL TRADING. The Rev. E. T. Reed and the Question.
div.p: MUNICIPAL TRADING. The Rev. E. T. Reed and the Question.

- -- Council Should Welcome an Investigation. On Saturaay evening the Rev. E T Reed, was elected President of the Warrington and District Union of Chris- tian Endeavour and le the course of his presidential address the rev. gentleman;referred to the principles of the Christian Eadeavour movement. The movement he said, stood for, good ;citizenship. Some of those present would know that this was a question of very great importance to them in Warrington at the present time, and there were members of the Union who by and by, if they were not so already, would become rate- payers of the town. There could be nothing that had more to do with the well being of a community than righteousness in public, life, and the recognition on the. part of those who were elected to the !Ts- , poosible positions of being governors of the town in which they lived of the fact that they were the servants of tloose who elected them, and that it was their bounden duty and privilege as those representatives, to be absolutely pure and above sus- picion in their:public actions. So let them (his hearers) see that so far as in them lay, their influence was used in that direction. " If the men upon whom the Govern- ment lot the town depends " continued Mr. Reed " are sincere in their professions of in- terest in the well beitig of the community they will see that no grounds for toe shadow of a sus- picion rest upon their actions. They will welcome the fullest investigation into the affairs of the town which, as the representatives of the ratepayers they have tem- porarily under their control."

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of the above Board was held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday.—There were present :—Messrs J Stokes (in the chair), A It Norman, J.P.C.C., (vice-chairman), the Rev Dr Gastaldi, Messrs S Taylor, J.P., T Lea, T Reynolds, T Wood, the mem- bers of the Rural Council, with Messrs G F Ashton (clerk), W E Hough (assistant clerk), and J Cunnah (master). TUE PROPOSED FIRE ESCAPE STAIRCASES. Mr Knollys, assistant secretary to the Local Govern- ment Board, wrote under data 22nd February, advert- ing to the letter of the Board dated 2nd December last, with reference to the proposed provision of fire escape staircases at the Runcorn Union Workhouse, and enquir- ing whether it was intended that such staircases should be placed in the positions which their inspector, Mr Dansey, indicated to the Guardians. The Board con- sidered that where sick or infirm cases might have to be carried downstairs, the staircases should be at least three feet wide, although a width of two feet might. suffice in the main buildings for the able-bodied, as the Board understood that the flights of stairs there were short. The Board should be furnished with a complete and detailed estimate of the cost of the work in the accompanying form, so far as it is applicable. Mr Mosely Williams said that the Visiting Committee had before them the recommendation and had unani- mously agreed to the proposed alteration by Mr Dansey, with respect to the width of th 3 staircase.

FINANCE. Mr Woodward reported that the payments for out relief were as follow:—Runcorn, £B5 ; Frod- sham, £25 ; Budwortb, £3O. The Cmnty rate was £3,049 184 which was a reduction of £207 for the corresponding period last year. Reftrence to the year book showed that that was the lowest call the County had made on that account Ginn Lady Day 1893. The rate was equal to 4.11,in the £. The general statement showed that the balance from the last meeting amounted to £7lO us 21 ; receipts, £2,177 7s 51; payments that day, £3.253 5+ 6d, which lett them with a deficit balance of £365 6i 9d. That was how the balance would appear on the books, but a cheque would be placed to their credit of £2,100 by the County Authority on account of salaries which would leave a balance in hand of £1,700. The report was approved. LITERATURE FOR THE INMATES. The following ladies and gentlemen, it was reported, had forwarded parcels of literature for the inmates for which the Guardians returned thanks :—Mesdames Whitley and Fletcher and Messrs Winfield and Board— man.

NUMB OF INMATES• Mr Moseley Williams reported on behalf of the House Committee that the condition of the House was very srtisfactory. There were 167 inmates in the house aa compared with 160 for that time last year. This concluded the businecs.

THE PROPuSED TRAMWAYS EXT ENSION. Opposition from- Stockton Heath. A special meeting of t- he Stockton Heath Parish Council was held on Thursday last week when tile proposal of the Corporation to extend the tramway system from near Stafford-road to Stockton Heath, and from thence along [Grappenhall-road to the Swing Bridge at Latchford,was considered. Mr Clarke preside and therewere also present:—Messr, [ Pearson, Whitley, Bouchier, Mclntyre, Pembertons Fairhurst and Bradshaw (clerk). 1 The Clerk reed a letter which he lied received from the Town Clerk of Warrington, stating that the Corporation would not agree to the following terms submitted by the Parish Council :—(1) That old London-road be widened to at least fifty feet, the metalled portion (from kerb to kerb) being say thirty five feet, and that two lines of rails be fixed ; (2), that the fare from Victoria-square, Stockton Heath, to Rylands-street, Warrington, be not mole than one penny ; (3), that the Corporation light the roads on which the railway is to run, and that except with the consent of the local authorities, the line be used for passenger traffic only ; (4)that any agreement for running powers with the Warrington and Nor thwich Light Railway should be for pasteager traffic only ex- cept with like consent. The Chairmen and the Clerk were instructed to represent the Council at the inquiry to be held on March 4th,and to ask that the Orier be not granted unless the above terms be agreed to.
